(C. - EX PROC. ROG. PANORMITAN., annis 1913-1927)

WITNESS I
Sr. GERONIMA MAZZA

Scope in the process: From Sess. 5th of 3 March 1913 (cf. Proc. f. 73) to Sess. 9th of 11 March 1913 (f. 122).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Geronima Mazza, born in 1855 at S. Benedetto del Tronto (Ascoli Piceno).

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior of the Orphanage of Castiglione.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: 23 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 47 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 58 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God on entering among the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza (1878), and then continued to follow the work of the Superior General as a member of the same Institute.

p. 566

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The first answers, containing already known information, are omitted, and the parts of greatest interest of the present testimony are reported: the action of the Servant of God in guiding the Institute; the heroic exercise of the virtues; the supernatural gifts; the widespread and ever-present reputation for holiness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 77, testis respondit:

§ 877
General details of the witness. She always looked after the spiritual and temporal good of the sisters.

My name is Sr. Geronima Mazza, born at San Benedetto del Tronto (province of Ascoli Piceno), domiciled at Castiglione di Sicilia, aged 58, I belong to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; Superior of the Queen Margherita Orphanage of Castiglione, daughter of the late Libero Mazza.

Ad 7: I first heard of Sr. Rosa Gattorno from a Missionary, on the occasion when, desiring to choose a religious Order, he suggested to me that of St. Anne. It was then that I came to know Sr. Rosa Gattorno at Piacenza.

Ad 15, Proc. fol. 84: The first directress of the Institute from its very beginnings was Sr. Rosa Gattorno, nor was it she herself who placed herself at the head of this direction, but she was placed by Authority, that is, by the Holy Father Pius IX; and this too out of a spirit of obedience, and always with a spirit of obedience she held it. She never ceased to direct the Institution. During the time that she governed the Institute, she always used prudence and charity in everything concerning her office.

She always watched over the good of the Sisters in everything concerning their spiritual and temporal good. As to the observance of the Rules, she was vigilant and always reminded the Sisters of the observance of the Rules, saying: «Daughters, if you do not observe the Rules you will not have the blessing of the Lord». And she was the first to submit to the Rules. When there was some fault, she corrected it with indulgence and charity; and, asked by me how this could be achieved, she answered: «When it happens that I feel indisposed, before making the correction I withdraw to my room, read a book, and then proceed to the correction».

§ 879
Charity toward the sick.

For the sick she had a great charity; one day, I know, on the occasion of a sick woman, she said to me: «Daughter, if you have nothing to give, rather sell even your shift to keep the sick woman well», and she added: «The sick Sister in a House draws down the blessing of God». And this sentiment of hers she communicated repeatedly to all the Superiors of the various Houses.

Ad 16: She observed all the Commandments of God and the Precepts of the Church scrupulously, as I have heard said and as is known to me from the time I knew her. She likewise observed the Vows scrupulously; from the time I was given to live with Sr. Gattorno, I can say that I found her most edifying in the observance of the holy vows, that is: obedience, chastity and poverty. I do not know whether she made other vows.

§ 880
Ardent and active faith.

Ad 17: She was animated by living faith in God, and this was manifested not only by deeds but also by words, and especially when she spoke of Jesus in the Sacrament, of the Most Holy Crucifix, of the Child Jesus, and it is proved by her having insisted with the H. See to obtain the privilege of being able to celebrate on Christmas Night the three Holy Masses in all the Houses.

She had a particular devotion to the Most Holy Trinity and wrote three prayers which are still recited in all the Houses. For Our Lady and St. Anne she cherished a most particular affection and devotion.

She was zealous for the Christian instruction of children and of the ignorant, so much so that for the instruction needed in the Parishes she gave us the obedience to go.

She attended Holy Mass every day and, after Holy Communion, remained an hour kneeling, prostrate on the chair, as I was able to observe many times. She had a most lively devotion to the Virgin Mary, who was her favorite. This devotion she inculcated in all the Houses. She had a special devotion to all the Saints, especially St. Anne, St. Michael the Archangel, St. Joseph, St. Francis of Assisi and St. Francis of Paola.

She had a particular devotion and reverence for the Supreme Pontiff, for Prelates and for Priests, and she instilled this same veneration in all the Sisters and in all the Houses, saying to the Sisters: «Remember, daughters, that they are the help of our Institute».

§ 881
Theological hope.

Ad 18: In all the circumstances of life she manifested hope in God and the desire for eternal life, and employed every means. From worldly and temporal things she had her heart detached, nor did she value them, and when she was in tribulations or anxieties and was ill, she bore all adversities with joy of heart, placing her hope in God. Nor did trust in God ever fail.

§ 882
She loved the Lord and was grieved to see that others did not love him.

Ad 19: She always loved God and felt grief on seeing that men did not love him. She had lively sorrow for the offenses that men committed against God, and I know, from having heard it said, that she scourged herself for the sins that are committed against God. After the prayers she had us recite an Our Father for poor sinners. And to me she once said: «Geronima, go on saying this Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory be for the conversion of sinners, which pleases the Heart of Jesus so much». When she received Holy Eucharist, I have already said that she remained in mental prayer; and she was solicitous to communicate this ardent love of God to all the Sisters; and to speak of the love of God was her food.

§ 883
She loved her neighbor with great love.

Ad 20: Toward neighbor she nourished a true spirit of charity; and it is shown by the fact that her Institute aims at all the works of mercy; it, for the deaf-mutes, for the blind, for the sick at home and in the hospitals, procuring for all social levels, in want, the spiritual good first and the temporal afterward. She worked with zeal for the conversion of sinners, insinuating herself directly or through the Sisters in order to obtain the salvation of souls. She instructed the ignorant, gave good counsel, consoled the afflicted and provided for the needs of the sick, the indigent and the poor. All these works of charity she fulfilled with lively ardor, and morning and evening she asked a minute account of how we had rendered our work to the sick.

Many enemies she had, because the works of God are thwarted by the world. But she knew how to suffer, to forgive injuries and even to love her enemies.

§ 884
Prudence in the discharge of her office as superior.

Ad 21, Proc. fol. 94: She was prudent in everything, and this prudence she showed in the acts of her life and of her administration as Superior: whenever the Sisters went to her in the difficulties in which they found themselves, the counsels, exhortations or admonitions they received from her were always inspired by prudence.

§ 885
Spirit of justice toward God and toward neighbor.

Ad 22: She was just in the sense of virtuous in justice, for all the commandments of God she observed and fulfilled, inasmuch as they aimed at the salvation of her soul, and also at the preservation of natural strength. And she was just also toward neighbor. When she bought something or received labor from workers or had to settle the just wage with servants, there was never a time that she did not pay what was due: she never used any overreaching; and as to debt, I do not know whether she contracted any; but I know for certain that, if so, she must have discharged it. I know, from having heard it said and because it is known to me, that Sr. Rosa insisted that if there were debts in the Houses they be paid at once, always exhorting the Sisters never to contract debts. As to relations with the constituted authorities, both civil and ecclesiastical, as far as I know, she never failed in either reverence or obedience.

§ 886
Spirit of penance and mortification. Fortitude in difficulties.

Ad 23: She was sparing in eating and in drinking very restrained. As to foods, as far as I know, I never saw her eat meat: an egg now and then, butter to season the soup, potatoes and fish was her ordinary food. As to wine, I never saw her drink wine, in the time I knew her; I do not know whether in the last times she was obliged to use it.

As to spiritual and bodily penances, I consider that they were in use by her: however I have heard that she had hair-shirts, but it is not known to me.

Ad 24: In the course of her life, especially in the administration of the Institute, she met many adversities; but she with a strong soul resisted and came out victorious. Human respect did not hold her back from doing good, and the anxieties of soul she patiently bore, on various occasions, in the various phases of life.

Ad 25: The Mother always loved Chastity. I know that she slept on a straw pallet and wrapped in two cloaks. This chastity she felt so much that she inculcated it in the Sisters, exhorting them to modesty of the senses, of the eyes, and in conversing, particularly with persons of the other sex.

Ad 26: She loved obedience, poverty and humility, and used to say to us: «Daughters, love poverty; if you keep the superfluous you will not be blessed by God».

§ 888
She practiced virtue in a heroic degree without excesses.

Ad 27: Of the virtues of which we have spoken and with which Sr. Rosa was adorned, it is my firm opinion that she had the exercise of them in a heroic degree. For it is true that one can be obedient, humble, poor, etc., but to the heroic degree, as these virtues shone in Sr. Rosa Gattorno, one cannot arrive without the special help of God.

Ad 28: She never went to excess in the exercise of these virtues, never gave proof of immoderate zeal, and if she mortified her body and did penances they were not such as to hinder her in the exercise of her delicate office as Superior, because she did all this at night, and then by day she was always at her desk listening to the nuns, etc.

Ad 29: I do not know whether she published books, treatises, booklets; I know, however, that she formulated prayers on the Most Holy Trinity, as I said above, and wrote countless letters. The prayers are in the little book of our prayers. Of the letters I too received some, but they are not at present in my possession, for I left them in the House at Pistoia. In my letters there is nothing against faith or morals.

§ 889
Prophetic spirit.

Ad 30: Being at Pistoia as Superior of the House, I was called by the Mother to Piacenza. I arrived at Piacenza at four in the morning. At nine o'clock I was called by the Mother for the audience. «Gerolomina», she said to me: «You must return immediately to Pistoia because there is a Sister there who is ill». Without more ado I had to obey and returned in the afternoon hours of that day. To my surprise I found that Sr. Anna Rufina, a pious and virtuous soul, had died. I had received the invitation from the Mother the evening before, and had taken the train at nine o'clock the same evening. I had left Sr. A. Rufina in her ordinary state, and I remember that that evening she had eaten peppers and tomatoes. I, surprised at the fact, asked whether perhaps the Sisters had sent a telegram to the Mother, and at what hour the Sister had died. The Sisters answered me that they had not telegraphed to the Mother, and that the Sister had died at nine o'clock, the hour when the Mother gave me the news of the Sister's grave illness.

§ 890
Reputation for holiness.

Ad 34: The reputation and opinion of the Servant of God was that she was adorned with special Christian virtues and supernatural gifts, and this while she lived; a reputation that lasts after her death, and that endures at so great a distance from her death, and that grows everywhere. And this is my firm opinion.

I know that she had enemies, as I said above, but they spoke out of passion, and among these must also be counted her relatives with regard to the house in Rome. But I am not aware that anyone spoke ill of the Servant of God and of the virtues that adorned her.

WITNESS II
Sr. ANNA TITA ARMELLINI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 11th of 28 April 1913 (f. 151) to Sess. 17th of 14 June 1913 (f. 218).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Tita Armellini, born in 1873 at Montalto delle Marche.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, local Superior.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: 15 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 57 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 40 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God at Ferrara, around the year 1888, then entered the Institute founded by her and maintained with the Mother Foundress the relations of subject to Superior, bearing in mind that the witness spent many years in Latin America.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: For the present testimony too we shall report, for reasons already specified elsewhere, only the parts of greatest note: the facts and circumstances that preceded the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; the way in which she interpreted the role of Superior General; the perfect observance of the theological virtues.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 153, testis respondit:

§ 891
General details of the witness.

My name is Sr. Anna Tita Armellini, daughter of the late Tito and Maria Antonelli, born at Montalto delle Marche, domiciled at Palermo, forty years of age completed, religious Daughter of St. Anne, indeed Superior of the Institute «Lancia Brolo» and in the economic conditions dictated by the rule.

p. 572

Ad 7: I heard, as a young girl, for the first time of S. A. Gattorno at Ferrara where I was. And not only did I hear her spoken of, but I knew her, because at Ferrara itself she received me as a Sister; and I was not more than fifteen years old.

§ 892
Works of charity after her husband's death.

Ad 13: During her widowhood, I know that she devoted herself to good and charitable works toward youth. She was also Superior of the Daughters of Mary at Genoa, and I know that at that time, for charitable ends, she began to think of the usefulness of an institute that would redound to the advantage of humanity. In this she followed the counsel of her Director and at the same time raised prayers to the Lord. I know that she met difficulties, not on the part of the Church, but on the social side, inasmuch as the aids necessary for her work were not coming to her.

But when she carried out the thought of the Institute in the first house at Piacenza she provided for the well-being of her children, placing them in religious institutes, and I remember that a deaf-mute daughter she placed in an institute for deaf-mutes.

§ 893
Foundation and prudent government of the Institute.

Ad 14: She founded the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne for the good of humanity, established it at Piacenza with good success, because from there it extended to many regions. She thought of giving rules to the Institute, and in these rules the bishop or her spiritual director may have had a part, perhaps because of the humility of the Servant of God in not believing herself capable of so much. This first form of rule was not approved by the H. See, but by imposition of Pius IX the Mother presented a new form of rule, which was approved. I gather the tradition that this second rule was written by the Mother. The Institute of S. A. Rosa Gattorno has had great development, and flourishes still. I say only that in the eleven years I was assigned to America there were few houses; and now there are several, that is about twenty.

Ad 15: She was the first moderator of the Institute. I do not know whether she spontaneously gave herself to this office or whether she accepted it out of obedience. We always remember her as Mother General of the Institute.

I do not know whether she renounced the office of Superior.

p. 573

She sustained the office with much energy, with wisdom, prudence and with much love. She always provided for the spiritual and temporal good of the houses. She scrupulously watched over the observance of the rule in all the houses, and always gave the example first of the observance of the rule. She corrected faults with much patience and charity, and showed great charity for the sick Sisters.

§ 894
Scrupulous observance of the precepts of God and of the Church.

Ad 16: I can testify that during the time I knew her I always saw her observant of the precepts of God and of the Church and observant of all the obligations of her religious state, in which I knew her.

She established as a rule the vows of chastity, of poverty and of obedience, nor can I testify anything against the observance of these vows on the part of the Mother.

§ 895
Apostolic zeal.

Ad 17: Both in speaking and in works she showed a lively zeal for the faith, instilling it in those who had it not, and for this she made every effort to bring about new houses in distant regions. She had zeal that the poor and the unlettered be instructed in the Christian catechism, and for this in our rule this catechetical instruction for the poor, for those in danger, is a cornerstone of our rule. She was carried away in a special manner by the mysteries of the Most Holy Passion and of the Most Holy Sacrament. I remember that, when I was a novice at Piacenza, on the days of Holy Thursday, Friday and Saturday, I saw her remain on her knees a very long time in the church, in a reserved part, and she left the Church last, which made a great impression on me; and I remember also that in these times of passion she withdrew into a small cubicle that was beside the choir; and it is my opinion, and I heard it from the sisters, that the Mother did penance there and remained fasting.

§ 896
Characteristic devotions.

As to the mystery of the Most Holy Eucharist, the Mother approached the altar with great fervor to feed on the Bread of Angels, and after having received Most Holy Communion, remaining to give thanks to the Lord, this fervor shone celestially from her face. Holy Communion she made at the beginning of Mass, and then assisted at the Holy Sacrifice with great devotion and recollection and always kneeling. The thanksgiving was prolonged not only for the time of Holy Mass, but also for quite a while after Holy Mass.

p. 574

The Mother always showed particular devotion toward the Mother of God.

§ 897
Reverence toward the Pope, bishops and priests.

She had most special reverence for the Roman Pontiff and for the Bishops.

A particular fact I can testify to. Being in a house in America, among the many that were there in Pará (Brazil), a superior of a house reported to me that, prompted by a regular ecclesiastic against the local Bishop, since he was pointed out to her as lacking zeal for souls, in good faith she thought to make a complaint to the H. See against the Bishop. This complaint will certainly have been sent to the Generalate House, because the local Superior added that she had received from Mother Gattorno a reproof for having put in writing an accusation against the Bishop and having sent it to the supreme authority, whereas at most the said Superior should have turned to the Generalate House, which, if the case required it, would have acted with prudence, because of the great deference and veneration that the Institute had to have for all Bishops.

As to Priests, I know that she always had the greatest respect. She inculcated in us due veneration for the Ministers of the Lord, and I say that nothing is known to me to the contrary.

§ 898
She loved and sought the goods of eternal life.

Ad 18: The Mother committed her whole life, spent in sacrifices, precisely to this lively hope of attaining eternal life; and she employed every means that might lead her to it.

The things of earth and temporal goods she not only did not love but despised, so much so that she left everything of the world in order to devote herself wholly and for her whole life to the good of the Institute, and she experienced anxieties and difficulties in bringing it into being, difficulties and anxieties which she bore with holy resignation.

The Mother, since I knew her, always had physical sufferings which, as far as she could, she often concealed in order to attend to all that was needed for the needs of the Institute. In the sufferings she experienced, whether of spirit and moral in bringing the Institute into being and propagating it, or physical, she always had great trust in God, and this trust infused in her lively courage to overcome every difficulty for the greater glory of God.

§ 899
She loved the Lord with great tenderness.

Ad 19: The Mother loved God with great tenderness. We always had great admiration for her. It is known to me that she took great care not to offend the Lord and desired that others not offend him.

I know nothing whether she felt sorrow for the sins men committed or strove to repair or expiate the said sins. However, during the Novitiate we went from one prayer to another for poor sinners, at the invitation and suggestion of the Mother.

As to prayers and the reception of the Sacraments, I can testify to what I said above, that is, that she did the one and the other with lively ardor.

This divine love the Mother also thought, with words and with works, to awaken in all of us. In the letters and in the conferences that she wrote or gave, she always infused in us this love of God.

§ 900
Lively charity toward neighbor.

Ad 20: The Servant of God was seized in soul by lively charity for neighbor, and the very foundation of the Institute demonstrates it, since this Institute has as its end the good, both spiritual and temporal, of neighbor.

Of special facts concerning her cooperation in the conversion of sinners, I can testify to the following: A person being in a private house in Piacenza gravely ill and near death and reluctant to be fortified with the Sacraments, the mother drew near to her and with lively prayers, with exhortations and with tears did so much with the help of God that that sinner changed his mind, confessed and received the Sacraments before dying.

WITNESS III
Sr. STEFANINA MARCOTTI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 18th of 20 June 1913 (p. 225) to Sess. 24 of 14 July 1913 (p. 275).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Stefanina Marcotti, born in 1859 at Cortemaggiore (Piacenza).

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, active at the Pignatelli Institute of Palermo.

p. 576

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 54 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness is not clear in delimiting the scope of her knowledge; in any case she had contacts with the Servant of God from her entry into the Institute and afterwards for several years.

Only a precious declaration of the witness is attached regarding the drafting of the Rules: the rest is omitted because it offers no new elements of proof.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 227, testis respondit:

§ 901
General details of the witness.

My name is Stefanina Marcotti, of the late Fortunato, born at Corte Maggiore, province of Piacenza, domiciled in Palermo at the Pignatelli Institute, aged fifty-four, religious daughter of St. Anne.

Ad 14, Proc. fol. 231: When I entered the Institute in 1875 I found a draft of a rule. I do not remember whether it was printed or handwritten. I learned afterwards from the Sisters living there that the Mother was working together with Fr. G. Battista Tornatore, whom I knew, on the reform of the rules, and a second draft came out of it. This new draft of the rule was also in use in the house, where it was read; I cannot say whether this new draft of the rule is the definitive rule that was afterwards approved by the H. See.

WITNESS VI
Sr. MARIA TERESA PATTI DI SORRENTINO

Scope in the process: From Sess. 34th of 30 October 1914 (p. 360) to Sess. 51 of 8 June 1915 (p. 490).

p. 578

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, born in 1861 at Palermo.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior of the Educational Institute of St. Anne of Palermo.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 54 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: For about 15 years excellent relations existed between the witness and the Servant of God, founded on mutual esteem, which enabled the witness to arrive at a thorough knowledge of the Servant of God. The witness, born Duchess of Sorrentino, died in the reputation of holiness: in his deposition, Card. Granito di Belmonte confirms the truth of this assertion (cf. Rom. Proc., witness I, fol. 146-146v.).

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: Sr. Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino in her deposition offers numerous and valid elements of judgment on the life and action of the Servant of God, and in particular on the heroic exercise of the virtues, as well as on the reputation for holiness and for supernatural gifts. For reasons of brevity, the reported information being already known to us, only the information concerning the heroic exercise of the theological virtues is reported here.

It must be borne in mind that the witness was not satisfied with the manner in which she was questioned, because the Judges showed excessive haste and did not reread her deposition to her: she asked for and obtained to be questioned in the Roman Process (cf. Rom. Proc., Sess. CCCXXXVI, fol. 2829).

Ad 2 interr., Proc. p. 361, testis respondit:

§ 904
General details of the witness.

My name is Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, of the late Francesco and of Laura Longo, born in Palermo, aged 54, and domiciled here, at the Educational Institute of St. Anne, where I act as Superior of the same Institute.

Ad 7. Having become a religious, I knew Sr. Rosa Gattorno personally in Rome.

§ 905
Full of faith and of apostolic spirit.

Ad art. 81, Of heroic Faith, Proc. p. 413: I can assure that the Mother always showed herself full of faith in all the individual truths of our holy religion. Several times I heard her exclaim: My Jesus has set my faith in diamonds, how I must thank him. These words she said with a fiery accent and with firmness.

She was anxious to teach the first rudiments of our Holy Religion to all, especially to poor children. And when she, because of her weak health, could no longer do it, she sent us Sisters to the Church every Sunday for the teaching of catechism. Such was her concern that several times I saw her in Rome watch from a small gallery the Sisters who taught Christian doctrine, even though she was very ill.

I saw her always most obedient to the Church, to the Roman Pontiff and to all Superiors. Toward Priests she was always humble and spoke to them with great regard, and this same she required of her daughters.

She was zealous for the decorum of the church, principally of those that belonged to her.

She was anxious to gain indulgences, and in the spread of the H. Faith she was most ardent.

Ad 82: Her heroic faith was manifested in her works, in her piety in serving God and neighbor with perfection.

§ 906
Love for the mysteries of religion.

Ad 83: Toward the mysteries of our Holy Religion she nourished special affection. Her daily practices of piety revealed her inner devotion and veneration for all that was of God.

She was penetrated to the highest degree with the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar. In spite of her continual sufferings I saw her almost always on her knees a long time after Holy Communion, which she never omitted, and she lived the whole day on this holy union with Jesus. She told me that even at night she prepared herself for the immense grace of uniting herself to Jesus in the Sacrament the following morning. There was no obstacle for her, and even after the long night journeys on which I accompanied the good Mother in the dead of winter, I never saw her omit Holy Communion, despite her not slight infirmities and her already advanced age.

§ 907
Eucharistic life.

Ad 88: I saw the Mother always pray with ardor before Jesus in the Sacrament. In her most urgent needs she ordered the Exposition of the Most Blessed Sacrament, and sent numerous Sisters in turn to the Chapel to pray; she insisted more when the grace she asked for herself or for others seemed hard to obtain. She herself spent long hours in adoration, and I saw her several times with love fix her eyes on the sacred host. As she herself sometimes told me, in those moments of adoration she saw inside the sacred host now shadows, now extraordinary light, now also signs. From these signs which Jesus showed her the Mother gathered good or painful events that were to happen far away or near. But she rarely spoke to me of this, and she herself made such statements to me following my insistence. After these communications with the Lord she remained as if absorbed and silent. She then repeatedly recommended that I not repeat to anyone the words that she had confidentially let slip. I do not know the special fact alluded to in the article. I add on my part that from elderly Sisters I have heard it told that the Mother, being in a Church in Genoa at a late hour before the Most Holy Sacrament, and hidden in a corner, did not hear the door of the Church being closed, and remained there all night.

§ 908
Most devoted to the Incarnation and the Passion of the Lord.

Ad 90: The Mother was most devoted to the august mystery of the incarnation and of the birth of Jesus Christ, and urged that its solemnity be celebrated in all the houses. Being too ill to make the holy crib herself with her own hands, she charged her daughters to make it «very beautiful», then came to see it with great joy. I do not know the particular fact alluded to in the article.

Ad 91: The meditation on this holy mystery consoled her greatly, and whoever was near her could perceive on her face an unusual joy. Also in the letters she sent to her distant daughters she showed herself happy for the feast, and it was dear to her to send to all the little picture with the holy child. I do not know the particular fact of the article.

Ad 92: The Mother continually meditated on the Passion of Jesus, even at night, as she herself told me several times. She was a lover of the Crucifix, always contemplated it and kept it as the perpetual model of her life.

Many times I saw her embracing the great crucifix she kept in her room, to implore relief, help and comfort in the most difficult and painful moments. Also in her letters she recalled Jesus on the cross and always concluded with this phrase: «I embrace you in my dear Crucifix».

Ad 93: The Mother pointed to the Crucifix to her daughters as the sole model, urged them to meditate before it to learn to love sacrifice and mortification.

I do not know the particular fact of the Article.

Ad 94: The Mother composed the little chaplet in honor of Jesus Crucified which is recited every day in the houses of the Institute. Several times she gave me to understand that she offered her sufferings to the Lord for the conversion of sinners.

On the last two days of carnival, in particular, she withdrew to pray and had the Most Holy Sacrament exposed in the chapel in reparation for all the outrages done to the Lord.

Ad 95: The Mother loved Jesus Crucified with all the strength of her heart and, in her poor little room in Rome, held dearest the image of Jesus Crucified that she kept on the table.

As to the long hours of rest she took upon a trunk of a cross, I declare that this has no relation to the furnishings found in the said little room in Rome. I can affirm nothing about the use she made of this trunk of a cross on which she lay down to sleep. But I know, having heard it from S. Benedetta Carrega, that this trunk of a cross was found in the house at Piacenza in a secluded little room on the second floor, where the Mother was accustomed to withdraw.

§ 909
Devotion to St. Anne and to other saints.

Ad Art. 98, Proc. p. 423: The Mother had intense devotion to St. Anne. As she had it in her heart so she had it on her lips, spoke of her with enthusiasm, instilling in the souls of her daughters this great sweet devotion.

Also in her letters she almost always named St. Anne and, placing in her the liveliest faith, always presented her to us as the most valid help for the progress of the Institute and as the strongest support with God. «St. Anne is a powerful old woman», she often repeated to us, her daughters, and she urged us to love her and venerate her greatly, and to draw her protection by exactly carrying out the works prescribed by our rule. I note that in our rules there is the obligation to take as first name that of Anne.

Ad 99: She was most devoted to all these Saints, but principally to St. Joseph, St. Francis of Assisi and St. Francis of Paola.

She suffraged the souls in Purgatory with special devotion.

Ad 100: She was always attached to the Apostolic See, to the Vicar of Jesus Christ, on whose nod she loved to depend, regarding the slightest disposition of the H. Father as a grave command.

p. 582

She rendered homage to the whole Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, and these sentiments of respect she instilled in the souls of her daughters.

§ 910
Very pious and a lover of prayer.

Ad 101: Since I knew her I was able to observe that the soul of the Mother was deeply pious, and she showed this by loving prayer, her chief nourishment.

Her ever recollected appearance revealed to all of us her continual spirit of prayer, habitual in her. Several times she told me that she had to do herself great violence in the parlor, and tried to avoid it when she did not see the need.

Ad 102: She warmly recommended to all her daughters prayer as the sole means to overcome temptations, obtain graces from God and reach eternal life.

I do not know the words written to her daughters at Piacenza.

Ad 103: I always saw the Servant of God desirous of spreading faith in the souls of her daughters and especially of the weaker and wavering ones. With her fiery words she encouraged all to remain firm in the liveliest faith.

§ 911
Trust and hope in the Lord.

Ad 104: During all the time I knew her I noticed in her a lively trust in the assistance of the Lord in all the works she undertook for the good, the growth and the erection of the various houses of the Institute. Nor ever, I can affirm in conscience, did I see her falter in spirit and strength to achieve the holy undertaking which she had set herself for the glory of God. Moreover I am convinced that on this hope, on the powerful help of God, the sublime inspirations of her good works were founded in order to gain as reward the Holy paradise. All her cares were directed to the acquisition of eternal beatitude, and therefore she consecrated to God her soul, her life, her possessions.

Ad 105: For this hope she abandoned everything to follow the voice of Jesus, breaking the most sacred earthly affections of daughter and of mother. She leaps over the body of her mother who, though a woman of strong piety, hindered her in her holy purposes. She flees from her father's house to please God.

Ad 106: The Mother always hoped in divine help and not in human aids, as she herself always told me several times. She then instilled this hope in God in all, especially in the Sisters, by word and in writing.

I do not know the rest of the article.

Ad 107: The Mother in acting always had in view to please God and to gain the holy paradise.

I do not remember the precise words that the article attributes to the Mother, but I remember that she spoke to us with similar phrases.

§ 912
Patience and fortitude in adversities.

Ad 108: The Mother had in God an unlimited confidence, and her trust in him grew all the more amid the disillusionments from creatures.

Several times, seeing her assailed on all sides and even betrayed by persons she had benefited, I asked her how she could still have trust: «I have trust in my Jesus, and that is enough for me».

I never saw her lose heart in any adverse circumstance; on the contrary, in the most unforeseen and difficult cases she reacted with a supernatural strength, and in these moments more than ever she had recourse to prayer. And I, several times in these circumstances, saw her come out of the Chapel tranquil as if nothing untoward had ever happened, smiling in her conformity to the divine wills.

The phrase that the article reports was habitual to her, and she repeated it also in her letters.

Ad 109: The Servant of God bore everything with patience, as I myself saw, and often with cheerfulness. She loved the straitness and privations of religious life, trusted in God and hoped everything from him.

The second part of this article, concerning the hardships experienced in the rise of the Institution, were reported to me several times by Sisters who were then with her.

Ad 111: The Lord rewarded so great an abandonment to him by granting his Servant extraordinary gifts, immense strength in the labors of her ministry at an advanced age and troubled by continual infirmities; she cared neither for sacrifices nor for weariness when need required it.

None of us Sisters could equal her in this strength of endurance. She herself noticed it, and many times told us jokingly: «The spirit is willing but the flesh is weary». But she always attributed her extraordinary strength to divine help, and often I heard her exclaim: «If my Jesus gives us the strength I will undertake that journey or do that given work».

Ad 112: The Servant of God, trusting in God, made the strength of the Lord her own.

§ 913
Singular charity toward God: union with God.

Ad art. 113, Proc. fol. 431: Mother Rosa Gattorno was singular in her charity toward God, loved the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity with intense love and composed a prayer in their honor. This prayer the Mother recited and had recited, and to this day it is recited in the houses of the Institute.

Ad 114: The Mother loved to remain a long time in prayer before Jesus in the Sacrament to open her heart to him and pray for the Church and for all.

Ad 115: Her recollected appearance revealed to her daughters her perfect union with God, and her words unveiled the great divine love with which her heart was inflamed.

She always spoke of her Jesus with emotion and with utmost rapture; also in her letters she did not write without adding some loving phrase for Jesus. Thus she wrote to Sr. Maria Clemens, now deceased, the following words, which I read: «Love God with a love all fire». And this she wrote shortly before the Mother died.

I do not remember the precise words cited in the second part of the article, but concerning the love of God the Mother always spoke to us in similar senses, and knew how to do so with such unction and effectiveness that she set our hearts aflame.

Ad 116: It is known to me that when she spoke of supernatural truths or of the divine attributes she spoke with enthusiasm until her face lit up. One may say that she lived on Jesus and could not detach herself from him.

§ 914
Spirit of continual prayer.

Ad 117: I saw the Mother act as if God had made himself master of the Mother's affections, and when she was occupied with her office she seemed always with her mind turned to God. Even outside the hours established by the rule she always prayed to him, whether at work, or in the customary actions of the day, in illnesses however grave, on journeys.

Many times she told me that she spent the nights in contemplation of heavenly things.

§ 915
Turned to heaven in mind and heart.

Ad 118: When, because of the occupations inherent in her office, she could not go to Church, I always saw her resigned, but her mind and heart seemed turned to God, and she gave more than ever vent to her love with pious aspirations.

I do not know the words cited in the second part of the article.

Ad 119: The Servant of God venerated with lively rapture of charity the Most Holy Sacrament of the altar. She spent long hours before the Holy Tabernacle. From elderly Sisters I learned that at the beginning of the foundation of the Institute she spent there also part of the night, always in prayer.

Ad 120: The Mother seemed always to meditate on the passion of Jesus. This practice of devotion saw its peak in Holy Week. From Holy Thursday evening to Saturday morning she remained shut in her room, without leaving it. I suppose that she accompanied Jesus in thought to Calvary.

I, on that day, did not see that food was brought to her in her room; I learned afterwards from Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, Secretary General of the Institute, that on that given day, she being shut in the room, no food was brought to her.

Interrogata respondit: As far as I remember, I spent three times Holy Week in the Generalate House in Rome.

When she came out of her room on Holy Saturday for the ceremony, the mark of a very great suffering could be seen on her face. I add that when Holy Week of the year 1894 came round, while she was staying in the new house in via D'Ossuna, where I was in charge as Superior, on the day of Good Friday she remained shut in her room; I, who was often near her room, did not notice that food was brought to her.

Ad 121: I learned from Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta that the Mother, at the beginning of the foundation of the Institute, reading aloud the morning meditation, point by point, concerning the Passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ, developing the subject, would be withdrawn from the senses.

§ 916
Devotion to the H. Heart and to Our Lady.

Ad 122: I always saw the Mother devoted to the Heart of Jesus, and this devotion she instilled in the souls of her daughters with words and with writings, encouraging them to suffer for love of the Divine Heart.

I do not know the words reported in the article. I learned, however, from the Mother herself that Sister Vincenza was her first secretary.

Ad 123: The Mother showed very great affection for Most Holy Mary, instilled devotion to her in all, especially in those under her, and was most anxious to solemnize her principal feasts with novenas in Church.

For the month of May and for the Immaculate Conception she ordered solemn feasts. To the Blessed Virgin under the title of Mary «Mater Gratiae et Mater Misericordiae» she dedicated the church following a vision which she herself related to me.

§ 917
Apparition of Our Lady.

Interrogata ex officio respondit: From the Mother herself I learned that following the difficulties encountered in the building of the Church of the Generalate House in Rome, this event befell her. On the very day on which all the difficulties for the rise of the Church had been smoothed over, entering her room she felt as if struck by a violent blow in her right side, so that, unable to stand, she collapsed on the bed. As the illness continued the doctor was called and ascertained that it was peritonitis. The matter being grave, she had resigned herself to die. Suddenly, on a day of the illness, this vision appeared to her: the Blessed Virgin holding in her arm Jesus, having in his hand a heart. Afterwards it seemed to her that the child Jesus no longer had the heart, but a chalice which he brought to the mouth of the Mother herself, making her drink something. The vision disappeared and she immediately found herself healed. I add that the Mother, while she told me this in her room, pointed out to me the right wall opposite her bed where the vision appeared to her. This, she added, was the reason why she dedicated the church to Mary «Mater Gratiae et Mater Misericordiae».

Ad art. 124, Proc. fol. 439: The Servant of God honored St. Anne worthily and zealously spread her cult among her daughters, whom she always placed under devotion to her. She held in honor St. Joseph, St. Francis of Assisi and the saints in general.

She had great devotion to the souls in Purgatory, for whom she often prayed and to whom she particularly commended herself. Every time she got into a carriage she recited a De profundis.

§ 918
Faithful to the divine precepts and horror of sin.

Ad 125: I always saw the Mother observe the divine precepts and those of the Church with diligence.

She was a model to her daughters in the observance of the H. Rules. In writing and still more by word she recommended to them to put them scrupulously into practice, and several times I heard her say that the exact observance of the rules of the Institute would suffice for a sister to become a saint.

Ad 126: I saw the Servant of God work in every way to prevent mortal sin. She grieved immensely at the offense of God, and on her face one could see the sorrowful impression her heart received from it. I was never present at a blasphemy uttered in her presence; several times I saw her mark her forehead with her thumb in the sign of the cross when she heard of an offense done to God, or of some sinner; often she exclaimed: «My Jesus, mercy».

She constantly recommended to her daughters to pray for the conversion of sinners and to appease divine justice.

Ad 127: The Mother abhorred venial fault, and I always saw her use every spiritual means to remove or avoid the offense, even the slightest, done to the Lord; this above all with her daughters.

I do not know the words reported in the article.

§ 919
Apostolic zeal for the conversion of sinners.

Many times I saw the Mother use every means to bring back to the right path the strayed and the lukewarm. Particularly with her daughters she never failed to correct them and to help them.

To bring souls back to God was the principal aim of her life, and her charity was therefore exercised in hospitals, orphanages, prisons, boarding schools, shelters, with the aim of skillfully directing souls to God.

Of heroic charity toward neighbor

Ad 128: The love of God was manifested in the mother by an extraordinary love toward neighbor, and I always saw her full of charity toward neighbor.

I do not know the details of this article.

§ 920
She lived only for God and for neighbor.

Ad 130: It seemed to me that the Mother lived only for God and for neighbor, almost forgetting herself in her life of complete sacrifice. Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega told me how at Genoa the Servant of God was already pointed out, as a layperson, as a consoling angel of the poor and the afflicted. Her lively charity increased as a religious, and for the time I spent with her I can affirm that she passed her life doing good.

Ad 131: It was habitual with her to procure the salvation of the soul of neighbor and in particular the spiritual salvation of the daughters of the Institute.

She instructed with love the ignorant in Christian truths and in Catholic morals, and for her there were no obstacles when it was a matter of preventing an evil or of converting some sinner. She counseled doubtful souls, and did so with such unction as to move hearts. This unlimited zeal she then poured out continually on her daughters, from whom she obtained promptly and surprisingly fruits of sacrifice, of repentance and of virtuous resolutions. This I was able to observe many and many a time being with the Servant of God.

A lover of peace, she sought to instill it in the heart of whoever approached her when she saw the need. She recommended that this peace be maintained in the communities dependent on her. She bore with resignation insults, betrayals, forgiving offenses with such generosity that I several times believed she had forgotten them.

§ 921
The poor, her beloved.

Ad 132: The poor were the beloved of the Mother in the exercise of her immense charity. She loved them, helped them with infinite tenderness in their needs, and recommended them to wealthy persons that they might come to their aid. In them she saw the image of God and, in imitation of the Divine Master, sacrificed herself for their good, instilling these sentiments of charity in the hearts of her daughters.

The sense of the words reported in the article is found in the rules of the Institute written by her.

Ad 133: From Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega and from other elderly Sisters I learned that the Mother, in the first years of her widowhood, voluntarily consecrated herself to God in the exercise of charity, serving suffering humanity by day and by night both in the hovels of the poor and in the Pammatone Hospital at Genoa.

Ad 134: I know that the Servant of God was at that time under the direction of the Archbishop of Genoa. She herself told me several times that he had given her many times further assignments.

Ad 136: The Mother told me that she had begun the work at Piacenza by gathering poor little girls, and that she was helped by the first Sisters to educate them and instruct them in piety.

Ad 137: From elderly Sisters I learned that the Mother, to meet the not few needs of all her works of charity, went to ask alms, not caring about the contempt she received and suffering many humiliations in silence for love of Jesus.

Ad 138: From elderly Sisters it has been reported to me that the Mother ran solicitously everywhere to relieve every sort of misery, encouraging her first daughters to follow her in these works of charity.

§ 922
For 39 years she governed the Institute with great charity.

Ad 139: The Mother for thirty-three years governed the Institute with charity, as I was told by elderly Sisters.

For the eight years that I was near her, I always saw her solicitous toward her daughters, immensely charitable in the care she gave them in soul and body; she lifted their spirits with sweet and comforting words and corrected them when necessary, even strongly, but always with charity. In illnesses she assisted them personally and from elderly Sisters I heard it told how she sent the nursing Sisters to rest, taking on all the work of care.

Ad 141: The Servant of God helped with great charity needy persons who did not dare to ask openly for alms. I saw the Mother take trouble to ask also for clothing from wealthy families to help the said persons secretly. She was full of charity for all, excused the faults of others, and often, not being able to excuse them, I saw her keep silent.

She was generous in forgiving offenses, and I always saw her return good for evil in order to be a faithful imitator of our Savior.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior of the Mother House at Piacenza. Quality of the witness: Eyewitness. Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: 33 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 36 years. Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 79 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God at Piacenza in 1867, the year in which she entered the recently founded Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; she declares that she lived with her 25 years and even more, though discontinuously.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: We

find ourselves before one of the first companions of the Servant of God, one of the Religious who was most at the side of Mother Rosa, to the point of attaining a high degree of knowledge, both from the standpoint of the succession of the events of her life and from that of her spiritual growth. Hence the precise information about her birth and family, the married period, the dedication shown in the role of mother, up to the examination of the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, of which she was provident Superior General from 1866 to 1900, that is, until her death.

The proofs concerning the individual virtues are also detailed, in which it is well demonstrated that the Servant of God raised herself supra communem operandi modum; the interesting deposition concludes with information on the illness and the reputation for holiness.

Ad 1 interr., Proc. p. 21, testis respondit:

§ 935
General details of the witness.

My name is Sr. Giuseppa Troni, daughter of the late Giovanni and the late Teresa Balestra. I was born in Cortemaggiore, in this Diocese of Piacenza. My domicile is in Piacenza, Stradone Farnese n. 49. I am 79 years old; I am Superior of the Mother House of the Daughters of St. Anne. Before religious profession I lived by my work.

§ 936
Accusations by Count Barbiellini.

Ad 3: By Count Gaspare Amidei Barbiellini I was accused before the lay criminal Court of having removed documents from the house of the aforesaid Count; but the accusation was stripped of all foundation, so much so that I was acquitted for non-existence of crime. Asked how the above accusation could have had any appearance, I answered: Between the Mother House and Barbiellini's dwelling there was an internal communication, and since Barbiellini was son-in-law of the Mother general and therefore in much familiar relation with our House, I sent the Sisters and sometimes went myself to do the cleaning in the Count's house, during, however, the absence of the Count himself and of his family. This happened in 1900, the year in which the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno died. The communication between the two houses existed before the death of Mother Gattorno and was closed by order of the Apostolic Visitor Mgr. Serafini, Archbishop of Spoleto, in the same year 1900. I must note that the Barbiellini family was composed of father, mother and several children of both sexes, of whom the eldest of the boys would have been about fifteen years old. The passage served the Sisters for going to the Barbiellini house, as well as the Barbiellini family for going to the Sisters' house. I note likewise that Mother General Rosa Gattorno was aware of the use to which the said communicating door served. I am not aware that any inconveniences were produced by this communication, which, moreover, was intercepted by a door locked with key and bolt on the inside of the Mother House.

§ 937
Knowledge of the Servant of God and veneration for her.

Ad 6: Without having expressly heard the name of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, she was however already known to me, and in this way: in the Collegiate Church of Cortemaggiore there was established the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, to which I too belonged. The said Congregation was established for the purpose of preparing vocations for a religious Institute which, according to the rumor that went about, was to be founded in Piacenza by a Genoese Lady, whom I afterwards learned to be Mrs. Rosa Gattorno; then, having decided to take the religious habit, I entered the said Institute, after conferences also with the aforesaid Lady. I am not aware that there are printed or handwritten biographies of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno.

I entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in the first days of April 1867. I lived intermittently with the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno for 25 years or perhaps even more.

§ 938
Family life.

Ad 7. I have the greatest veneration for the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, because I always knew her to be of blameless and holy life and because she loved me and esteemed me much. I most greatly desire that she be inscribed as soon as possible in the album of the Saints. Not being able to do anything else to this end I raise prayers to the Lord that he may be pleased to glorify this his faithful Servant. Ad 8: The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, as far as I know, was born in Genoa, in her father's house, on 14 October 1831. I do not remember the name of the father of the Servant of God, but I knew him personally, as also personally I knew the mother, Mrs. Adelaide Campanella. They were more than well-off persons, and above all of good morals and God-fearing. I know that they had other children, of whom I knew three. All were educated in a Christian manner.

Ad 10, Proc. p. 26: She spent, as far as I know, her childhood and adolescence with her own parents. I do not know whether she learned letters or some art proper to the feminine state. Since I knew her she was always a model of a daughter toward her own parents. I cannot attest whether in her early youth she loved solitude, silence and mortification of herself, nor whether even then she gave signs of special fervor of spirit. I know, however, that she was Directress of the Ladies of Charity and applied herself, in private houses and also in hospitals, to the assistance of the poor sick.

§ 939
Married life and children she had.

Ad 11: Solely to obey her own parents and follow the counsel of the Confessor she chose the married state. In the will of her parents and in the counsel of the Confessor she saw clearly in this the will of the Lord. I do not know how she previously disposed herself for this state. The husband of the Servant of God was Girolamo Custo, her cousin; I do not know whether the husband was a truly God-fearing person. I suppose so, since the Servant of God accepted his hand.

She had several children: I knew two: Alessandro and Carlotta. She placed Carlotta, who was deaf-mute, in an educational Institute in Milan, and her son Alessandro in a College of the Barnabites.

The Servant of God, as far as I know, always fulfilled the duties of a mother. I do not know how long she lived in marriage. After her husband's death she gave herself to a life of greater Christian perfection, exercising herself, as I have said, in the assistance of the sick, who greatly loved to be assisted by her.

Ad 12: I do not know whether and with whom she took counsel before undertaking

§ 940
Foundation of the Institute and placement of the children.

the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. I am convinced, however, that through fervent prayer she will have asked the Lord for light in the matter. I do not know whether she met obstacles or difficulties in carrying out her plan. Meanwhile, her work having been put into execution, she provided for her son Alessandro by placing him with the Colli family of Piacenza, a family which, as far as I know, was honored and honest. Her daughter Carlotta, having left the Institute at Milan, was kept with the Mother in this Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, and remained here until she married. I note, however, that attached to the House of the Daughters of St. Anne, indeed in the same house, the Servant of God had opened a girls' school which numbered 70 and more girls, especially orphans.

p. 600

Ad 13: From my own knowledge I can assure that the Servant of God was truly the foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. She founded the said Institute with her own means and with those gathered from the daughters who joined the Institute and from benefactors.

The first house founded by the Servant of God was this one, in via Stradone Farnese, formerly the Dal Verme palace. As soon as this Institute was opened it had many vocations. Subsequently Houses were opened at Cento, at Sampierdarena, at Genoa and afterwards in other cities of Italy and abroad, as in South and North America, in Austria etc.

§ 941
Drawing up of the rules.

The rules of the Institute were drawn up by the Servant of God, and their aim is especially the exercise of works of charity toward the sick of whatever illness and condition, the education of youth, schools etc.

I learned from the brother, indeed it was told me that a brother of the Servant of God reported that the Servant of God was withdrawn forty days in fasting and prayer to compose the rules of the Institute. These rules were approved by the local Ecclesiastical Authority, as I suppose, and afterwards received solemn confirmation from the H. See and precisely from H.M. Leo XIII.

The Institute had extraordinary growth and brought forth abundant fruits everywhere, especially in Hospitals, asylums and schools. The Institute was always in flower and even at present continues to develop, and no year passes without nine to ten Houses being founded. Many too are the vocations, notwithstanding the wickedness of the times.

§ 942
Prudent and charitable government.

Ad 14: The Mother Foundress Rosa Gattorno was the first Superior General, and this by command of the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX. The government of the Institute was held by her from 1866 to 1900, that is, until the time of her death. She fulfilled her Office always well and with all prudence: she always wisely provided for the spiritual and temporal good of the Daughters of St. Anne. She watched attentively that the rules of the Institute be observed, preceding her Daughters by example. She took care to correct the faults she was able to perceive, never failing either through too much severity or through too much indulgence. In a special way she showed her charity toward the sick Sisters, founding for them various houses of care and lavishing on the patients the necessary assistance as to body and as to spirit. I know that one of these Houses is in the Province of Piacenza, one in Naples, a third in Naples, indeed in Palermo.

Ad 15: Since I knew her I never saw her voluntarily transgress the precepts of God and of the Church, nor did she ever fall short of the obligations of her state. She made the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, fulfilling them exactly.

§ 943
All the virtues shone in her in an eminent manner.
§ 944
Devotions, divine worship and Eucharistic life.

Ad 16, Proc. p. 30: Of my own knowledge I can attest that in the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno the theological and cardinal virtues shone in an eminent manner, and also all the others that constitute Christian perfection. She burned with the desire to spread the faith, as her words and her works showed. Often she urged this virtue on her daughters and, precisely to spread it, she founded the Institute, sending her daughters to the Americas and to Africa, where they run schools in which native boys and girls are instructed, to many of whom they often confer Baptism. The Servant of God also cared for the teaching of catechism by opening a nursery school in this city, precisely opposite the Oratory of Death, where the children learned to read and write and were instructed in the things of religion, and the Servant of God supplied free of charge to all the poor children what was needed for school. This school lasted about 15 years, that is, until special circumstances, independent of the will of Mother Gattorno, determined its closing. The Servant of God showed particular devotion to the First Person of the Most Holy Trinity: indeed she wished that the first month of the year be consecrated by us to this August Person, in which month every day special prayers are made and benediction is given with the Most Holy Sacrament. Likewise she showed special devotion to the Most Holy Crucifix. She always carried it closely at her side, and so great was her devotion to the Crucifix that when speaking to her daughters or giving them warnings and corrections she always did so recalling the sufferings that Our Lord underwent for us.

She took very great care of the splendor of divine worship and wanted the functions to be carried out with decorum. For the feast of St. Anne she extended a general invitation to the Priests of the city to come and celebrate in the Chapel of the Institute. She showed particular faith and devotion toward the Most Holy Eucharist, both by receiving it daily and by spending long hours at the Holy Tabernacle; every Sunday and every time she felt the need of some particular grace the Servant of God wanted the Most Holy Sacrament exposed for the whole morning, duly authorized for this by the diocesan Ordinary, and she recommended to the Community to approach Holy Communion, and she herself stayed before the Most Holy Sacrament exposed from 7 to 12 o'clock, during which time she did not want to be called elsewhere in order to remain solely in adoration. Moreover she ordered that her daughters, four by four, make about an hour of adoration. With special devotion and recollection she assisted every day at Holy Mass. And when she could not attend the Community Mass, she expressly had a second one celebrated in order to assist at it.

Every day she made the visit to the Most Holy Sacrament, which she prolonged for some hours; she had great devotion to Mary Most Holy Immaculate, striving to instill it in others also. She took much care also of the cult of the Saints, and in particular of St. Joseph, St. Francis of Assisi and St. Francis of Paola.

Above all, however, she wanted her daughters to show great devotion to the Protectress St. Anne, to whom she dedicated the Institute.

The Servant of God showed herself an always submissive and affectionate daughter of the Roman Pontiff, spoke of him to her daughters with great respect, and recommended that every day prayer be offered for him, and this she also placed among the exercises of piety that her daughters must perform daily. She showed equal affection toward the Church, the Episcopate and the Catholic Priesthood, and every time the Church suffered some tribulation or pressure she had particular prayers raised to the Lord.

§ 945
Virtue of hope and trust in God.

Ad 17: Great likewise in the Servant of God was the virtue of hope, showing great desire for eternal life, of which she often spoke to her daughters, and directing all her actions to this end. She greatly feared the pains of Purgatory and earnestly recommended to her daughters to pray to the Lord that after her death she be exempt from them in order to be united immediately to her God. She cared not for worldly things; rather she felt detachment from the world. Although at the beginning the Community found itself in some financial straits, the Servant of God never failed to hope in Providence.

§ 946
Charity and life of prayer.

Ad 18, Proc. p. 34: Her charity toward God was truly ardent. She showed singular concern never to offend the Lord, and also that he not be offended by others; if she knew him insulted she showed great sorrow, seeking to repair the affront with lively prayers. By order of the Servant of God, in our community prayers are said every day for the conversion of sinners, that is, in the common acts of piety.

She loved prayer much, both vocal and mental; indeed in the first years of the foundation of the Institute she taught her daughters and the girls of the school the practical exercise of meditation, and afterwards she made the meditation together with her fellow sisters. So she continued until a few years before her death.

She also strove with all diligence that this charity toward God be spread in others.

§ 947
Charity toward the poor and the sick.

Ad 19: She was also animated by the liveliest charity toward neighbor. To no one did she refuse the mite of her charity; she sent aid even to the homes of the poor and especially to the sick, whose assistance at home is precisely one of the aims of the Institute. The assistance of the Sisters to the sick has not only the aim of the health of the body, but also, especially, that of the soul. As far as is within my knowledge, none of the sick assisted by the Sisters died deprived of religious comforts. She exercised herself in all the works of mercy, both temporal and spiritual. Several times I saw afflicted Sisters who, after having conferred with the Servant of God, returned consoled.

She had lively devotion also for the Souls in Purgatory and by her order the pious practice of the month of November is celebrated in this House. When any Sister of this Order dies, three Masses are celebrated in the House where the death occurs, and by the Community three Communions are applied and three Rosaries recited, and in all the other houses of the Institute for the same purpose one mass is celebrated, one Communion applied and one Rosary recited, and this by order of the Servant of God.

Ad 20: Concerning the virtue of prudence, I have no reason to say

that she failed in this virtue.

§ 948
Relations with her relatives in Piacenza.

The witness being questioned about the relations of the Servant of God with her relatives living in Piacenza, she replies: The Sisters frequented the house of her son-in-law Count Barbiellini, also during his stay in Piacenza, to render some passing service, and especially a Sister went there to give piano and study lessons to Barbiellini's girls, and this by order of the Servant of God. Likewise the Servant of God sent me to assist her son Alessandro Custo, living in this city in Via Vescovado, during his illness of which he died. At first I went alone; afterwards I was accompanied by another Sister, or, I not going, two other Sisters went; the Servant of God did this to induce her son to receive, before dying, the Holy Sacraments, from which unfortunately he had lived estranged, and to avoid that the son's house be frequented by irreligious persons of bad conduct. In general the Community was content with the government of the Servant of God, who looked after its prosperity and always with acts informed by prudence. I know that distinguished persons, among them Princess Di Fitalia, went to the Servant of God for counsel and comfort, as also Countess Caracciolo, Marrazzani and others of this city. The Servant of God used no partiality toward anyone.

§ 949
Spirit of justice toward God and toward neighbor.

Ad 21: The Servant of God also practiced the virtue of justice, both toward the Lord, loving him supremely and observing his commandments with all diligence, and toward neighbor, giving each his own. In particular she was generous with workmen, to whom she abundantly granted their wages. She did not violate the good name of neighbor, she left no debt after her death. She showed herself obsequious not only toward ecclesiastical authority, but also toward civil authority. She contracted a debt for the building of the Generalate House in Rome, but secured the creditor with a mortgage on the Gargatano estate, a debt that is being paid off in installments.

§ 950
Spirit of mortification: balanced and serene.

Ad 22, Proc. p. 38: The Servant of God, as to the virtue of temperance, I can attest that she always ate meatless meals, but I do not know whether she did so for mortification; likewise she never drank wine; only in her last years did she take a little white wine.

I never saw her altered — when she spoke — moved by anger, but she spoke with zeal, animated only by the good of the Community.

§ 951
Secret instruments of penance.

She led a mortified and penitential life, fasting every day on the prescribed days, and living temperately in food and drink on all the other days of the year. From the bearing of her person, from the movements the Servant of God made, one could infer that she wore instruments of penance. She slept in a wretched little room, the barest and most uncomfortable in the House, of which she herself always kept the key, never allowing anyone to enter. From this the Community inferred that in that room the Servant of God kept instruments of penance with which she chastised her own body. These suspicions became a reality for us when, she having passed to a better life, it was possible to enter the said room. I myself having received the key, which was sent to me from Rome by the new Superior General with the commission to see whether in that room was to be found the Crucifix enclosed in a case, which case was given to the Servant of God by Princess Fitalia, the Crucifix which, according to what the Servant of God herself declared, had addressed some words to her, I was greatly surprised to find the room full of instruments of penance. A large cross formed of two beams, evidently made by the Mother herself, on which Cross the Servant of God climbed, fastening her wrists with iron devices; another cross stretched over a small bench, on which she lay, as is presumed, wearing the habit of a Franciscan Tertiary, found in the room. On the pillow she used a thick iron chain was sewn, on which it is inferred she rested her head. She slept on the straw mattress without mattress and without sheets, with a simple blanket. In the same room were also found several scourges with sharp iron points, hairshirts also formed of wire with points, which from their shape it is understood she put on her arms and on her sides, and other instruments such as a crown of thorns, cords with iron points, etc.

There are also found in the said room cloths stained with blood; sometimes the Servant of God was seen to appear before the Community with her face and forehead with small wounds from which blood came.

§ 952
Strong and serene in difficult moments.

Ad 23: As to the virtue of Fortitude I can attest that the Servant of God in moments difficult for the Institute showed herself strong and firm in bearing contrarieties, as happened at Bassano Veneto, where a certain Mgr. Chemin, still living, sought to remove subjects already belonging to the Institute in order to place them in another Institute. She never gave signs of impatience. Without human respect she faithfully fulfilled her duties.

p. 606

Ad 24: As to chastity, the Servant of God, as I can attest, always showed herself modest in words, in glance, in manner, and in illnesses she never permitted her body to be uncovered by the doctor or even by the sisters, applying the remedies herself, such as poultices etc.

Although in the last years of her life she was afflicted with swelling in the legs and feet, she did not permit others to help her put on her stockings. According to the circumstances she spoke with love of this virtue, recommending it to her daughters.

Ad 25, Proc. p. 42: As to poverty I can attest that the Servant of God showed herself in all her acts detached from the goods of the earth; she wore patched habits and her bearing was lowly, that of a poor religious in everything; so too she practiced obedience toward legitimate Superiors, nor am I aware that she failed in this virtue.

By acts and words she gave to understand that she held the virtue of humility very dear; she called herself by names that indicated contempt for her own person. In everything, forgetful of herself, she sought the glory of God. For as long as I knew her she was always an example and teacher to her daughters concerning this virtue.

§ 955
She exercised the virtues in a heroic degree.

Ad 26: In my opinion the Servant of God exercised all the said virtues in a heroic degree, inasmuch as I never saw her fail in them and also none other of us practiced them in so perfect a degree.

Ad 27: Although, as I have said, she exercised the above-mentioned virtues in a more perfect degree than her daughters, yet she did not go to excess in the exercise of them, letting herself, for example, be dominated by immoderate zeal, or exceeding in mortification so as to render herself unable to fulfill her own offices. So, for example, a few months before her death she still went to visit the houses of the Institute.

§ 956
Death and burial.

Ad 31, Proc. p. 45: The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno died on 6 May 1900 in the Generalate House in Rome, in Via Merulana n. 177, fortified with all the religious comforts and the Blessing of the H. Father.

Ad 32: As soon as she died, her body lay exposed, I believe for three days, indeed for two days. The funeral was celebrated in the Church of the Generalate House, and the body was provisionally interred in Campo Verano; then after a few years, I think after two years, it was transferred to the tomb expressly built for the Community of the Daughters of St. Anne in Rome. To her funeral much people flocked, and I heard on that occasion, being present myself, that it was said: a saint has died, and our benefactress.

§ 957
Held in repute as a saint in life and after death.

Ad 34: As far as I can attest, both in life and more so after death, the Servant of God was held in repute as a Saint. I myself consider her truly such, having observed no defect in her. I could not point to any person who does not rejoice that the present process is being held so that the Servant of God be raised to the honors of the Altar. A grace from the Servant of God I myself received after her death; as I already said, I was accused before the civil criminal Court of having removed documents in the Barbiellini House, fraudulently breaking open doors and the cabinet which contained the said documents. I commended myself to the Servant of God that she might bring my innocence to light, which I could not so easily have proved. My prayers were granted, so that I was acquitted for non-existence of crime.

Proc. p. 48: Iudices sequens quaesitum protulerunt: The witness being asked by the Most Rev. Judges whether she knows that Fr. G. Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission of St. Vincent de Paul, was treated by the Servant of God in a not quite correct manner, she who, forgetting how much Fr. Tornatore had done for the benefit of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, then invited him to withdraw from the House and no longer to concern himself with the Institute itself, replied: I am not aware that Fr. Tornatore ever received wrongs from the Servant of God; rather I can attest that during his stay in the House at Piacenza he was always treated with the regard due to his age and to his person.

§ 958
Clarifications about Fr. Tornatore.

The witness being asked whether it is true that Fr. Tornatore is the true Founder of the Daughters of St. Anne, she replied: I have never heard from anyone, nor have I reason to affirm, that Tornatore was Founder or Co-founder of our Institute; I can say rather that I heard several times Fr. Tornatore himself declare publicly that he was not our Founder, but that the Foundress of our Institute was the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, for whom he urged respect and gratitude.

General details of the witness.
