Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: It is only for reasons of objectivity that we have given space also to the present testimony; note how the criticisms leveled at the Servant of God — until now never endorsed by any other witness — are amply offset by the judgment on the virtues and on the reputation for holiness: both entirely positive.

Ad 1 interr., Proc. fol. 68, testis respondit:

§ 960
General details of the witness and veneration of the Servant of God.

My name is Sr. Anna Ferdinanda Denti, in the world Teresa, daughter of the late Antonio and the late Giovanna Monteverdi, born at Ripalla Guerina, Province of Cremona, on 11 April 1854. I live at Lodi and am Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne in the House of Lodi.

Ad 6: Before becoming a religious I never saw the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, nor heard of her. Having entered this House of Piacenza I heard Gattorno spoken of with great veneration.

Ad 7: I have great veneration for the Servant of God; however, I never turned to her with prayers to obtain heavenly graces and favors; rather, I correct myself: sometimes I prayed to her after her death to obtain some grace, but I was not heard. This veneration in me is produced more than anything by the great esteem in which she is held in the Institute of St. Anne. I too desire that she be declared blessed and to this end I join the Community in raising prayers to the Lord. I must correct myself: I hold the Servant of God in esteem also from my personal experience and knowledge of her, whom in all things I always found a person wholly of God.

§ 961
Relations of the Servant of God with her children.

Ad 12, Proc. p. 70: I must add that I myself saw her daughter Carlotta, married Barbiellini, enter the Institute accompanied by the wet nurse carrying in her arms the infant Maria, nursing; this did not make a good impression either on me or on some other Sister; all the more since the thing happened while the Servant of God was in this house. It also happened to me several times that, being Superior at Lodi and coming to the Mother General for counsel and comfort, during the conversation, the daughter Carlotta coming in, the Servant of God would dismiss me at once without my having been able to set out my affairs, and so I returned disillusioned and dissatisfied. I have heard that the same happened also to other sisters.

As to the son Alessandro, I have heard it said by trustworthy Sisters that the Servant of God sent two Sisters to assist the said son when he was ill, and one of these Sisters, as a reward, as it was said, was made Superior of the House of Genoa, where she remained until she left the Congregation to return to the world.

§ 962
Prudent government of the Servant of God.

Ad 14: The first General of the Institute was the Servant of God. I do not know with what authority she assumed the government of the Institute itself, which she held until death and which ordinarily she fulfilled well: it seems to me she always conducted herself with prudence.

She also provided for the temporal and spiritual good of her Daughters. I must not hide, however, that sometimes I was reproved because in the administration of my House I could not every year make the savings she demanded be handed over to her; and as she was cheerful and expansive when one had the good fortune to bring her some saving, so she showed herself dissatisfied and somewhat restless when one could hand over only a little.

She watched that the rules of the Institute be observed, indeed she preceded all the other sisters by example. She corrected the faults she could perceive in her daughters, letting herself be guided neither by excessive zeal nor by too much indulgence.

I must note, however, that the Servant of God too had her personal sympathies, for example in receiving the Superiors of the various Houses. Some she kept in audience, and for a long time, in preference to others whom, scarcely received, she soon dismissed. So in recreation she approached some in preference to others, and spoke to them with greater expansion of heart; these things were noticed by me and by another Superior.

The Servant of God was anxious that the sick sisters be cared for with all charity; she recommended the sick to the respective Superiors that nothing be lacking to them. This I can attest of my own knowledge.

Ad 16: In my judgment, in the Servant of God the virtues, both theological and cardinal, were outstanding.

§ 976
She founded the Institute with the sole aim of the glory of God and the good of souls.

Ad 13: She laid the first foundations of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne here in Piacenza with the sole aim of giving glory to the Lord and of procuring the good of souls; since her means were not sufficient, at the beginning, with another pious person, namely the now deceased Mistress Onorata Colli, she went about asking alms in the principal houses of the City. The Institute soon had great growth, notwithstanding the painful circumstances in which it found itself. Soon it spread, one may say, to almost all regions of the globe. Even at present it is much in flower, so much so that new Houses are continually opened, doing good everywhere.

I have heard from the elderly Sisters contemporary with the Servant of God that she, in the doubts and in the grave difficulties in which she found herself, especially at the beginning, had recourse to the H. Father Pius IX, of h.m., from whom she had fatherly counsel and ample support. He himself prophesied to her that her Daughters would multiply like the sands of the sea. She also had valid support and counsel from Fr. Giambattista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission of St. Vincent de Paul; I do not know precisely by whom the rules of the Institute were dictated: these, in any case, after 25 years of happy trial, were definitively confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff Leo XIII.

§ 977
Always and in everything she governed as a prudent superior.

Ad 14: I know that the first General was the Servant of God. I have heard it told that she received this office from Pope Pius IX. She held this office until death, never resigning it, although several times she had shown the desire and the will to do so. In my judgment Mother Gattorno in her office of General always and in

everything conducted herself with prudence.

As to the door of communication between the Barbiellini part and the Institute, I heard from Mother Gattorno herself that she had had permission for it from Pius IX. However, the opening of the door of communication was not looked on with favor by the Community, because through it entered not only the Daughter of the Servant of God but also the son-in-law Count Barbiellini, who went up also to the upper floor of the House to converse not only with the Mother but also with the Sisters who were closer to the Mother herself, perhaps to gain support from her. I can, however, attest that when Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, disapproving this communication, ordered the Mother some years before her death that the door be closed, the Mother obeyed promptly.

§ 978
She preceded all the sisters by example.

As far as I know, I believe she always provided for the spiritual and temporal good of the Sisters, and watched attentively that the rules of the Institute be observed. Every year she sent out a circular to all the Houses, recalling especially the observance of the Rules. She took care to watch over the Houses themselves, sometimes arriving by surprise to ascertain better the reality of things.

She preceded all the Sisters by example, especially in the spirit of mortification. Though she wanted the exact observance of the rules, she did not exceed through too much severity. A great spirit of charity animated her, especially toward the sick Sisters. She rose at night to assist them and see whether they lacked anything, and encouraged them to bear infirmities with patience and resignation.

§ 982
Relations with family members.

Ad 12: I knew the daughter of the Servant of God, Carlotta Custo, married Barbiellini. Sometimes she came with her husband to dine in this House without invitation. The Mother showed displeasure at this, and once she had me take the little pot off the fire while I was preparing the meal for them.

These visits of the Barbiellini family to the Mother were frequent, indeed one may say daily. The Sisters complained and also Mgr. Scalabrini had ordered that the two doors connecting the Barbiellini house with the Institute be closed. The Mother did not have the said two doors closed, because Barbiellini did not want it and opposed it energetically. However, the said two doors were always closed and the Barbiellini family could not enter the Institute unless a Sister went to open with the keys that I kept. Immediately after the death of the Servant of God, that is two or three days afterward, the doors in question were walled up in the presence of some Sisters, and I saw this too. Count Barbiellini, husband of Carlotta, opposed this energetically, bringing a complaint against the Superior Sr. Giuseppa Troni.

I also heard complaints from the Sisters and also from the poor and from lay persons because, it was said, the Barbiellini family lived at the expense of the Institute. To explain better the overbearing manner that Barbiellini showed toward the Institute, I add these facts: One day in the autumn of 1896 or 1897, Barbiellini, irritated I do not know for what reason against his mother-in-law Sr. Gattorno, accompanied his wife and the two daughters, keeping only the boys for himself, to the Institute to the Servant of God, saying that she should see to maintaining them; then he spitefully shut the door and withdrew into his house. Carlotta and the daughters were forced to remain in the Institute for 15 days, until a way was found to satisfy Barbiellini. Another day, about the same period as above, the Mother Superior Sr. Giuseppa and the Sister Secretaries and the Superior General Sr. Gattorno went to the country, to the villa of Gargatano, leaving me the express order not to open in any case the two doors of communication. Some hours after the departure of the said Superiors, I heard the bell that was at the aforesaid doors ring several times. I did not answer either the first or the second ring; but as the knocking went on so loudly as to threaten to break down the doors, I was forced to open, and then Carlotta came in with her eldest son, about 15 years old. Carlotta, as soon as she learned that the Servant of God was absent, withdrew and only the son remained, who, having seen the Sisters go down to the cellar, followed them and carried off a bottle of wine which he went to drink at home. The Mother General when she came to know of this fact scolded me, reproaching me for having opened the door, and it seems she scolded the daughter too, because she showed herself very dissatisfied with me and with the Sisters who had reported the fact to the Servant of God.

From the whole I can in conscience attest that Mother Sr. Gattorno did not approve of Barbiellini and his family frequenting the Institute so often, and if she allowed them to enter the Institute itself so frequently through her, she did so solely because she feared Barbiellini's violence and the consequences of the scenes that would inevitably have come. I note also that the Servant of God, especially in the last years, recommended to the Sisters that when Barbiellini or his wife, her daughter Carlotta, entered the Institute to speak with her, they should never leave her alone and should always keep an eye on Barbiellini.

Lastly I note also that the Sisters, at least once a year, when Barbiellini returned from Rome to settle in Piacenza, entered his house to carry out the cleaning of the rooms and furniture. And to do this they used the key of the Barbiellini house, which he himself handed over to the Superior Sr. Giuseppa.

§ 997
The witness does not hold a high opinion of the Servant of God.

Ad 7: Given the circumstances in which I found myself in the Institute, I cannot have a high opinion of the Servant of God. And here is the main reason. After three years of stay in the Institute, I was sent as Superior to the House of the Daughters of St. Anne at Ovada, or rather at Nizza Monferrato, then at Ovada, and afterward in other Houses. Several times I had to deplore that the Superior General Sr. Gattorno gave greater credence to the assertions of subordinate Sisters than to the reports of the respective Superiors. I was Superior at Pisa and was sent as Visitor to the House of the Daughters of St. Anne at Orbetello, to watch over the conduct of the Superior of that House, without the accusations concerning that Superior being specified. I stayed there about fifteen days, keeping her continually under observation and also asking about her secret information from the Ecclesiastical Authorities and from the Administrators of the Hospital of Orbetello, in which hospital the Daughters of St. Anne were serving. Not only could I perceive nothing irregular, but from everyone I had good information. Having reported the outcome of my mission to the Superior General Sr. Rosa Gattorno, I received in reply a letter written by the Secretary Sr. Carrega and bearing the signature of the Servant of God, but I am not certain that this signature was authentic. In that letter I was called a second Judas and an accomplice of the Superior of Orbetello. Since I was convinced that the letter in question, although written by the Secretary, had been seen and approved by the Superior General Sr. Gattorno, even if the signature was not authentic, I considered myself greatly offended by that expression and left the Institute after taking advice. I note that when this happened I had been fifteen years in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

§ 998
Fr. Tornatore co-founder of the Institute, according to the witness.

Ad 13: It is my opinion, and I have heard it said also by others, that Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore was the Co-founder of the Institute of St. Anne. He presided at the Chapters, it was he who imposed the penances on the Sisters. The Servant of God always had recourse to him for counsel. It was also said that Fr. Tornatore had

p. 633

composed some drafts of Rules for the Institute, without ever being able to obtain the superior approval.

§ 999
According to the witness the Servant of God did not govern the Institute well.

Ad 14: First General of the Institute was Sr. Gattorno. I do not know by what authority she assumed the government; I believe it happened naturally. I am not aware that she ever resigned the same office. In my opinion she did not always fulfill it well. For example, when I was Superior at Girgenti and needed to speak to the Servant of God on urgent and delicate matters, I wrote beforehand that I would come personally to her at Florence, where she then was. I did in fact go there, but I was not allowed to speak to her or even to see her, and the Secretary Sr. Carrega told me that the Mother was not well in health; I, however, heard her laughing and speaking with other Sisters, conversing with them. I was told to go to Rome and wait for her there. So I did, but also in Rome I could not have a private audience, although she had seen me and knew also my need. Once also in Sicily she dispatched to me from the mainland two Visitors to verify, as one of the said Visitors, a confidante of mine, told me, whether I kept a death's head in my room. I do not know whether this was the true motive of that visit, all the more so since the visit was personal and real and extended to all the persons and to the government of the House.

§ 1000
Several accusations against the government of the Servant of God.

Proc. p. 234: While I was at Nizza Monferrato I had under my direction a Sister who at another time had been my Superior and who, writing to the Mother, I gathered was accusing me of various faults, some even grave. The General having come to Nizza, under the promise of giving me some rest, took me with her to Piacenza. After about twenty days she appointed me Superior in the most important House, that of Ovada, and there a letter reached me from Fr. Tornatore in which I was accused of deeds that I did not know I had ever committed during my stay at Nizza. For the time being I kept silent, but afterward, the Mother General having come to Ovada, I showed her the letter mentioned, at the same time professing myself innocent of all that was charged to me. I had this reply from her: Pay no attention: Father Tornatore is mad. I note that in the government of the Institute such tricks were used. I recall this other fact. At Ovada, always under the pretext of rest, I was replaced in the office of Superior by a Sister who had taken the habit the day immediately before and who was said to be the niece of a Cardinal. After several months this Sister, promoted Superior at Sampierdarena, ran away after a while with a doctor of that Hospital in which the Sisters Daughters of St. Anne were serving. I add that sometimes I received from the Servant of God the order to send Sisters out to beg for the needs of the Institute; and if disorders then occurred and these were notified to her, she either did not reply or replied that I should not have sent them out to beg. Of this I speak from experience, and the facts I have narrated happened before 1892. It also seems to me, in my judgment, that the Servant of God did not always provide for the material needs of the Institute. When I was at Pisa, Superior of that House about 1880, we were thrown into the street by the owner of the premises we lived in. We were eleven Sisters without roof and without food. I wrote to the Superior General Sr. Gattorno setting out our great needs and she sent me no help, and recommended that I do the best I could, resorting to Divine Providence. The Servant of God, personally and through Fr. Tornatore, as I gather, often asked for money from the various Houses. The one who asked directly for money was generally Fr. Tornatore, certainly with the connivance of the Mother. The worst is that money also had to be sent to her son (Sr. Gattorno's), Alessandro Custo, who was a spendthrift; I note, however, that the order to send money to Custo did not come from the Mother General but from her Secretary. The sum sent was then not to be recorded; once when I noted it as sent to Custo, I was for this reproved by the Secretary herself, Sr. Carrega. The aforesaid Custo Alessandro, who was then about 17 years old, came every day to the Mother House of Piacenza, where he took food, not however with the Community. He also used overbearing acts toward the Sisters, wanting at once what he asked for; indeed once he became very impatient with me because, having ordered me to prepare a chicken for him, just taken from the coop, after half an hour it was not yet roasted. By his conduct he gave occasion for grave murmuring in the Community, and also squandered the goods when he had the administration of the Institute in his hands, as I was told after I had left the Community.

Proc. p. 237: As in the previous Session, I must

§ 1001
Communication of the Barbiellini house with the house of the Institute.

note that during my stay in the Institute I heard not a few complaints from the Sisters about the communication of the Barbiellini house with the Institute, or rather the Mother House of Piacenza, by means of two doors. Those of the Barbiellini family often, so to speak every day, came into the Sisters' house, as some of these entered the Barbiellini house. It was said that the daughter of the Servant of God, named Carlotta, when near childbirth, had to be surrounded by comely Sisters, so that, thus impressed, it might benefit the child to be born. I do not know whether this order properly came from the Mother General. A girl having been born, I saw the Sisters holding her in their arms, carrying her into the garden, in short caring for her, performing the office of nursemaid. I heard one of them complain about this more than once. I add also that the lamented Bishop Mgr. Scalabrini, after giving a course of H. Spiritual Exercises at the Mother House of Piacenza, to which on the occasion all the Superiors of the other Houses came, made the proposal, as commissioned by the H. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, to aggregate the Institute to some other already approved by the Church, but found opposition in the majority, and this especially from the General Secretary Sr. Carrega, who assured that it was the wish of the Servant of God that the Congregation founded by her should remain autonomous. I also heard it said on that occasion that Mgr. Scalabrini had also proposed that the communication of the Barbiellini house with the Sisters' House be removed, and that Sr. Carrega, in the presence of the General Sr. Gattorno, replied: You, Monsignor, must not meddle in these things.

In fact the doors remained open. It was a complaint, I would say almost general, that she used preferences and showed favoritism. The complaints were especially these: that she was surrounded by some favorites, while the others could rarely have an audience with the Servant of God.

§ 1002
Accusations of different treatment for some sisters.

Another complaint was the different treatment used for some; I mention one fact only. A young woman of Lodi entered the Institute with a rich and fine trousseau. She was told by the Mother that precisely because of its fineness this trousseau was not to be used in the Community. This same person after not long discovered that her linen was being used by Sr. Carrega and marked with the number two; astonished, she made remonstrances to the Mother General, who I do not know what she replied. In my opinion the Servant of God in the government of the Institute erred rather through excessive indulgence, letting certain things pass which then gave rise to grave disorders. Sisters without spirit were sent to the Houses, without having first undergone the due novitiate, so that the outcome of these dispatches could not be more unhappy. Sr. Gattorno was, however, a person of charity, taking care of the sick Sisters.

§ 1003
Eucharistic devotion: edifying conduct.

Ad 16: The Servant of God showed devotion to the Most H. Eucharist, she received Communion every day, keeping an edifying conduct. After Communion she remained in devout thanksgiving, at times even for some hours. When she could not go to Church because ill, she had herself taken, or rather went supported by the Sisters. One thing, however, that I did not like is that sometimes the whole Community was deprived of Communion as a punishment for a fault committed by some Sister; all the more since the nature of the deed was not always known. I must, however, point out that the order to abstain from Communion was given by Fr. Tornatore, but in the presence of the Mother General. I heard her speak with great veneration of Pope Pius IX, of h.m., and of the Supreme Pontiff in general.

§ 1004
Sobriety in food.

Ad 22, Proc. p. 240: She was sober in food, which she always took meatless, but I believe seasoned with butter. She used eggs; she did not drink wine. I saw her sometimes take a little vermouth, but out of need. I note, however, that she rarely went to eat in the refectory with the Community; she went to the second table to dine alone, or with some Sister. In the first three years that I was in the Mother House of Piacenza, sometimes the Servant of God called me near her private room, without however letting me enter, and handed me her linen, ordering me to go over it before handing it to the laundry: I noticed on that occasion that it was stained with blood, and I think that blood was drawn from her body with hairshirts or other instruments of penance.

§ 1005
She was not always victorious over herself.

Ad 23: In my opinion she was not always victorious over herself, sometimes giving way to outbursts of impatience, when she was embittered by the conduct of her own daughter Carlotta or of the poor girls who came to the Institute.

As pantry-keeper I had prepared a small meal for a Lady who had come to visit the Mother General. When I went to the pantry I noticed that there was nothing left; even the salt was lacking, although I had warned the local Superior of this several times so that she would provide. When the moment came to present the food to the Lady, there being nothing left, as has been said, the Servant of God became very upset and sharply reproved the local Superior and the Mother Secretary.

Ad 24-25: I do not even doubt that she loved chastity and guarded her senses. As to humility, it seems to me she never distinguished herself. Personally she loved poverty, but did not make this virtue observed so much by the Sisters who in a particular way surrounded her and whom she favored.

§ 1006

Ad 26: It does not seem to me that Mother Gattorno exercised the virtues to a heroic degree. Ad 34: I repeat that it is my opinion that the Servant of God is not a Saint for the Altars, and I believe my opinion is shared also by other persons.

§ 1011
Foundation and title of the Institute.

§ 1012

Ad 19: In my judgment Rosa Gattorno had no charity toward Fr. Tornatore; indeed I add that she showed herself ungrateful toward him, from whom the Institute had so many and many benefits. I have also heard that he was driven out of the Institute itself out of a feeling of jealousy. He, because of his virtues, had very great ascendancy over the Daughters of St. Anne, which was not looked on with favor by Gattorno. Fr. Tornatore, with regular permission of his Superiors, lived in the Houses of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza and at Rome, where the Mother General was. Whereas before he had from her and from the Sisters so many signs of deference, they then began no longer to show him due regard. I narrate this fact. One day I went to find him at Rome, precisely in the House of the Daughters of St. Anne in Via Merulana, and to my great surprise I found the poor old man confined in a wretched little room above the organ of the Church, to which room one gained access by an awkward staircase. I asked him why he no longer used his apartment, and he answered, spreading his arms and lifting his eyes to heaven: Dear son, the will of God must be done. Not long after, Cardinal Alimonda let him understand that his presence was useless, and Fr. Tornatore then added: Eminence, if that is so, I can go away; and without more ado he took his things in a handkerchief and went to the House of Montecitorio with his Confreres of the Mission. From then on, as far as I know, Sr. Gattorno had no more relations with Tornatore, and did not remember him even when the Father died, for whom nothing was done but one office in his suffrage in the House of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza, because it was imposed by Mgr. Bishop Scalabrini.

§ 1013
General details of the witness, sister of the Servant of God.

My name is Elisa Gattorno, of the late Francesco and Adelaide Campanella, born at Genoa, in the Parish of Our Lady delle Vigne, seventy-nine years ago. I am the widow of Angelo Savignone. I am a housewife. I live in Genoa, Via Bernardo Strozzi 5.

Ad 7: I knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno intimately, because she was my sister, with whom I lived until my eighteenth year of age. When she was married she went for some months to Marseilles, from where, having returned, she came back for about two more years to her father's house in Genoa. Afterward, on various occasions, having stayed with her, already foundress of the Institute, at Piacenza and then at Rome, I had occasion to be with her.

§ 1014
Family life.

Ad 9: Rosa Gattorno, my sister, was born in Genoa, I believe in the Parish of Our Lady delle Vigne, some six years before me: I am not able to specify this date better: of the common parents already named, Francesco and Adelaide Campanella. My family was exemplarily Christian and of civil standing. She was baptized in the Church, I believe, of delle Vigne, she was given the name Rosa. I do not know whether she had other names. I do not know exactly how many children my parents had. Living ones I knew six, three males and three females. At present three of us survive: a brother and two sisters. The upbringing, in the family, was Christian for all, since my mother especially was a holy woman, and was at the same time an upbringing such as befits a family of civil standing. The boys attended the public schools. For us girls, suitable governesses came to the house. All these things I know from direct knowledge, given my living together in the family. Other things I do not know for now.

§ 1015
Married on the advice of her parents.

Ad 11, Proc. fol. 20v.: On the advice of her parents she decided to marry at about nineteen years; I do not know whether she asked the Confessor's advice about this. She had been asked for by the celebrated Lawyer Orsini, and by a cousin of ours, Custo Gerolamo. She would have preferred the cousin; nevertheless, to comply with Papa's wish, she had consented to marry Orsini. The latter, then, by his conduct, and with trivial pretexts prolonging the conclusion of the marriage negotiations, displeased Papa, who no longer admitted him to the house. This being known, the cousin Custo renewed the request, and the marriage was concluded, the due dispensations for the kinship having been obtained. The marriage was celebrated at home in the afternoon, according to the custom of many families of that time, and the following morning, in the Chapel of the Sacristy of S. Lorenzo, the Spouses received the blessing and heard H. Mass. It seems to me that Rev. Fr. Accinelli, one of the vice-parish priests of the Metropolitan, was present at the wedding. Both in the one ceremony and in the other, the Servant of God had a modest demeanor and showed a joyful spirit without letting herself be carried away by joy.

§ 1016
Good wife and mother.

Ad 12: She loved her husband in a Christian way and was fully in accord subject to him, preserving — as far as I can know — honesty in marriage and taking great care of the house. She had three children: Carlotta, who became deaf-mute when very small, Alessandro and Francesco, who died after six or seven months of life.

She took care that they received, as soon as possible, H. Baptism; Carlotta she sent to the College for Deaf-Mute Girls in Milan, and she took care that Alessandro grew up in the fear of God and frequented the Holy Sacraments, and he was afterward also placed in the Seminary.

§ 1017
Life of prayer and penance after her husband's death.

Ad 14: To the present question I can answer from having heard it from papa and mamma, because I was then away from home: that Rosa, immediately after her husband's death, gave herself to praying much at night and doing penances, so that her father was displeased at it, telling her that she must nourish herself more and preserve herself for her children, and among other things he forced her to drink a little wine. She then began to frequent the Hospital.

§ 1018
Reputation for holiness.

Ad 35, Proc. fol. 29v.: I know that she was and is held as a holy soul by the unanimous judgment of all who spoke to me of her, also persons of high standing, among whom I recall the Princess of Fitalia, of Palermo, who also donated an altar for Our Lady of Lourdes for the Institute.

For my part, I consider that my sister Rosa was greatly virtuous, leaving it however to God to know the degree of holiness.

Mr. FRANCESCO GATTORNO

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 37, testis respondit:

§ 1019
General details of the witness, brother of the Servant of God.

My name is Francesco Gattorno, of the late Francesco and Adelaide Campanella, born at Genoa, parish of S. Maria delle Vigne, aged 74, married, landowner, living in Genoa, via Tommaso Reggio 10, 2.

Ad 3: I do not frequent the Sacraments, because my ideas in this regard do not allow it; I believe in God, but I do not consider these practices necessary.

In this regard my testimony on the life of my sister may have its value, because, notwithstanding her religious ideas, I nevertheless esteemed her greatly and always esteem her, and she was always conciliatory toward me, although she did not let slip any occasion to insinuate her beliefs to me.

Ad 7: I knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, because she was my sister. What I know and shall depose, either I knew directly or I heard from a person of the family, especially from papa and mamma.

I also read a biographical sketch, I think printed at Palermo by a certain Lombardi, and I found it very exact.

Ad 8: I esteemed and loved my sister and naturally would be glad that her virtue and her merit be recognized.

Ad 9: My sister was born in 1831 in the parish of Our Lady

§ 1020
Birth, education, family life.

delle Vigne in Genoa, and I believe that she was baptized in this Church, because from the Archive of the said Church I extracted a birth certificate. In this parish we were all born, brothers and sisters; except perhaps the first, because my father lived in the Lamba Doria palace, opposite the Church of delle Vigne. We were three brothers and three sisters, Rosa included.

Ad 10: She had from her parents a careful religious upbringing.

As a child she had an excellent disposition and was docile toward her parents as well as toward others. She went frequently to Sturla, to her grandmother's, who would always have wanted her with her. At Sturla she lived near the Church of the Annunziata, which was greatly helped by my grandfather, who was buried there.

§ 1021
Works of piety and charity after her husband's death.

Ad 13: Her husband died, I think, in 1857, or rather some years later. He had gone for some years to Russia, to Berdinuska, to a trading house of her brother-in-law Federico Gattorno. During her husband's illness she gave him loving assistance; she saw to it that he had the religious comforts and a funeral befitting his condition. She felt extraordinarily the grief of her husband's death; she returned to her father's house, because her father-in-law Custo did not want to care for the family left widowed, preferring other brothers, and therefore our family took on the commitment of placing the little orphans suitably.

Ad 14: After her husband's death, Rosa gave herself to extraordinary works of piety and charity, especially going to the Hospital of Pammatone. At first she acted by her own judgment, then she put herself in relation with Mgr. Charvaz, Archbishop of Genoa, and with Fr. Firpo, her Confessor, who guided her in her works of piety and beneficence. Several times I saw the Priest Firpo, who came to our house for this purpose.

§ 1022
Foundations and family conflicts.

Ad 15, Proc. fol. 42: I heard several times at home, from my sister, especially with mamma, about the foundation of an Institute; likewise I saw several times come to the house and stay a long while with my sister the widow Mrs. Morasso and Miss Rapallino, daughter of Mr. Rapallino, Cashier at the Discount Bank, and various other young women who afterward were my sister's companions in the Institute. Once I accompanied my sister to Pietrabizzara in Valle Scrivia, where she conferred with a Religious, who I think was called Cogrosso. I do not know whether and to whom she had recourse for counsel, but she was strongly resolved, very sure about the foundation.

Ad 16: I know that the first house of the Institute was opened at Piacenza, stradone Farnese; that she went there with Morasso, who had various means at her disposal, to arrange the rent of the House, which was afterward in part purchased.

She had difficulties, also on the part of mamma, who grieved at her daughter's departure; but she overcame everything with strength of soul. Afterward I learned that also at Piacenza she had very strong struggles, by which she was never cast down.

§ 1023
Title and habit of the Institute.

Ad 17: I do not know that the Institute had any other title besides that of Daughters of St. Anne. My sister put on the habit some short time after her companions, because at the beginning she had to travel, and it was the time of the war of 1866. From the very beginning they at once occupied themselves in the Institute with the care of the war wounded; and going once to Piacenza, I saw that they were busy preparing lint.

As to the form of the habit, my sister told me that she had chosen it because it was simple and modest and also convenient in price. At first they bought cloth from abroad, which for that reason was very expensive. I busied myself, with a traveler of the firm Rossi of Schio, so that in that weaving mill they would make a corresponding cloth. After some trials it succeeded, with great advantage to the Institute, as the Sisters assured me. In this regard I must testify that my sister, besides the occupations of religious life, directly managed the whole administration of the Institute and of the single Houses.

As far as concerned me, who was in business, I also put the Institute in relation with various commercial firms for the supply of provisions. I also busied myself, at her request, with the purchase of the site in Rome, in via Merulana, for the construction of the Generalate House, which she began with great courage in 1883. For this purpose I opened credit in my name in their favor with the Bank of Italy, besides with the Tiberina Bank, for the purchase and the advances. I know that in the archive there are all the records and contracts of this business. My sister showed in all this administration an extraordinary activity and an uncommon sagacity. When I went to her for these affairs, ordinarily she had already settled in her mind the plans to follow, which I, as a man of business, found well made. In two things we had some difference, which however ended as she wished; the first was that she always forgave those who did her harm, it seeming to me that for this reason they took heart to attempt other swindles. The second difference occurred on the occasion of a grave illness of mine, because, being the main holder of title of the building in via Merulana, I wanted to divest myself of this title, also destroying what was effectively mine, so that in the event of my death no confusions would arise between what belonged to the Institute and what would have gone to my children. My sister did not show herself disposed to this, because of the trust she had in me, and because she said she was sure that I would not die of that illness.

§ 1024
Activity and sure sagacity of the Servant of God in business.

To demonstrate my sister's activity and sure sagacity also in business I add that, having received from the Counts Caracciolo as inheritance an estate in the district of Piacenza, she wished, avoiding the tenant farmer, to manage it directly, which proved advantageous, though she afterward had to leave it, returning to the tenant farmer, to avoid thefts. Thus she bought from the Messrs. Carenzi of Sampierdarena a building, where she founded a College, paying for the said building 90 thousand lire, which some years ago was sold for half a million. The negotiations for the purchase of this building were conducted by me.

§ 1025
Exemplary life before marriage.

Ad 18, Proc. fol. 46: It seems to me that my sister's life can, for greater clarity, be distinguished into three periods: the first concerns the time before her marriage; the other, her married life; the third, the period of time that passes between the foundation of the Institute and her death. As to the first period, besides what I have already deposed in answering the preceding questions, I must add that my sister, as soon as she was of age, and before being placed in marriage, was like the soul of the paternal home. I recall, both from having observed it and from having heard it from mamma, that she, with an activity and self-denial worthy of every praise, performed for the most part the domestic duties, devoting to these all the time apart from that in which she attended to her own instruction.

My mamma suffered from frequent attacks of suffocation; the sister immediately younger than Rosa was frail, also as a consequence of a surgical operation in which she was assisted by Rosa; the other sister was still very small. Moreover there was at home the maternal grandmother, in need of continual assistance because of age; and there were still at home two brothers younger than she and the eldest, and therefore she had to bear continual and heavy work. This she bore without any complaint, with an admirable diligence, so that everything at home proceeded in order, nothing was lacking to anyone and, especially with the old grandmother and then ill until death, with mamma in her sufferings, with the frailer sister and with all of us she lavished the most loving care. So that her departure from the family was for it a grave loss.

She distinguished herself by her spirit of charity; she liked to make directly herself certain distributions to the poor customary in the family; everything she could dispose of she gave to the needy, and especially at the «bocchetta of S. Francesco d'Albaro», where the family went to the country, she was sought out by all for her charity. Even afterward, and for many years, they asked me, gratefully, for news of her.

§ 1026
Good wife and mother. Marital sufferings.

The marriage was downright a disaster, and the cause to my sister of continual sorrows and sacrifices. The hoped-for happiness went away with the car-

riage of the wedding journey.

We accompanied her for a stretch, that is, as far as Varazze, on the wedding journey; then, we relatives having returned home, she went on to Nice and Marseilles, where her husband's financial failure awaited her. She at once appealed to Papa, who ran to Marseilles to bring, in that desperate case, that help which was still possible, thus managing to save some small thing from that financial shipwreck, and then had to bring his daughter back to Genoa with her husband, receiving them in the paternal house.

There the misfortune awaited her of her first little girl being born deaf-mute; her husband, about 1855, went to Russia to work in a Trading House set up by his brother-in-law and my brother, and from there returned about 1857 already ruined in health, and in fact died of tubercular pneumonia before 1859.

In all these trials I was able to observe, together with her deep sorrow, her unbending strength of soul. She suffered especially for the deaf-mute little girl who, being ill, could not make her illness understood, expressing herself only with cries and tears.

She had to part from her, placing her in the Biffi Institute of Milan. In her husband's illness she was always ready to assist him day and night with every sacrifice. She would have wished to educate her children beside her; but it was not possible for her to keep her daughter with her, since the greater good of the latter required placing her in Milan, as I said. The son, of a rather lively disposition, having grown somewhat bigger, she could hardly manage to tame; she admonished him with kindness, but in vain; to have recourse to the grandfather to punish him her spirit could not bear. She therefore decided to entrust him to educational institutes, and he was placed first in the Seminary in Genoa, then in the College of the Missionaries at Savona.

As for the third period, that of religious life, I can depose nothing as regards that strictly religious life; I must, however, make known some things that concern my sister in family relations. The daughter, her education completed, desired to be placed in marriage, which was arranged in Rome and then celebrated in Genoa, in the paternal house which had passed into my ownership, where I lived together with my mother. The said marriage was concluded in 1876; for the religious marriage there came to the house Rev. Accinelli, custodian of the Metropolitan of S. Lorenzo; for the civil marriage there came the Marquis Negrotto, Mayor of Genoa.

§ 1027
Grave sorrows because of the daughter's marriage.

The daughter's marriage was the cause of numerous and grave sorrows.

In prosecutione expositionis iam inceptae, Proc. fol. 50, testis deposuit:

Rosa gave her daughter a dowry of about eighty thousand lire, securing it on a building in Sampierdarena, which had come to Rosa by paternal inheritance. Since at the time of this marriage my sister was somewhat short of cash, I met the expenses of the marriage and also gave what was needed for the wedding journey. Suitable gifts were made to the bride by relatives and friends of the family; I, together with my brother, gave two diamond earrings.

The spouses settled in Piacenza, where Rosa was also then resident, where they bought, paying at once an installment of the price, a small cottage with a little garden around it. Rosa constituted the aforementioned dowry by securing it on the building, because at the time of the marriage it was not possible to realize the value of the building suitably, which afterward, by an agreement with the Railway, was sold for about one hundred and twenty thousand lire. The transaction having been liquidated, the dowry was invested in a holding at Podenzano, in the Piacenza district.

My sister having thus fulfilled her duties as a mother toward her daughter, she should, at least for this part, have had no troubles; but the matter went very differently.

The daughter, incited and pushed on by her husband, sought to obtain advantages not only from her mother's family property, but also from what, through the work of the Sisters, was being accumulated in the Institute through donations. My sister, just as she had scrupulously given her daughter what could be due to her of the family property, so wanted rigorously preserved to the Institute what belonged to it.

She thus had to resist for many years the unjustified insistence of her daughter, who seized every occasion, spied on every moment to find herself alone with her mother in order to repeat her requests. I myself in Rome many times attended my sister's little meal, she being already in poor health, in order to free her by my presence from her daughter's annoyances, at least for the time of her very small repast. My sister never wished to yield on this point; I know, however, that the daughter obtained something from Mother Carrega — who however gave from her own personal goods — and perhaps from others, who tried by these means to appease the daughter for the good of the mother. But in vain, since the daughter, and perhaps more the son-in-law, with all their maneuvers during my sister's life, tried to gather the elements to bring suit against the Institute after Rosa's death. The said suit was in fact brought, pursued by every means and with all obstinacy; it was lost a first time by the daughter and son-in-law, was then resumed and again lost, in the Tribunal as well as in Appeal and in Cassation.

§ 1028
Sorrows caused by her son Alessandro.

She had no lesser sorrows from her son. He, corresponding little or nothing to the education he had received and to the family traditions, made little good success. At first he never managed to settle himself stably; he then went to Buenos Aires, where he stayed about two years. He then returned to Italy, stopped in Florence two or three years, afterward looking after a small paper mill on the Liri; he finally went to Piacenza, where he died, assisted by his mother, shortly after 1890. He, to obtain from my sister consent and help to contract marriage, confessed a fault not committed and the consequent paternity of a child. Before his death, however, he revealed to his mother that he had deceived her regarding this paternity and that the child was not his at all. Thus my sister had to suffer painful vexations from her daughter-in-law, who among other things obtained provisional seizures and even a search in her mother-in-law's room. She therefore had to defend herself to protect the Institute and to sustain the case for the disavowal of the legitimacy of the supposed grandson. I learned from various Sisters that in these straits my sister felt very great sorrow. In this case of disavowal I also intervened as a witness, and was able to show with irrefutable documents that for more than two years before the birth of the supposed grandson Rosa's son had lived uninterruptedly in America, while the woman always lived in Florence. In this suit too my sister achieved full victory, which however did not lessen her sorrows.

Antequam testis ulterius interrogetur, Proc. fol. 62, declaravit: I recall that I deposed in one of the first questionings that Rosa was baptized in the Church of Our Lady delle Vigne because, having had to extract several certificates from that archive, it seemed to me I had also extracted the baptismal certificate for Rosa. Thinking it over better and reviewing the family papers, I realized that the aforesaid baptismal certificate was extracted from the parish archive of S. Donato. It should be noted that the family formerly lived in the parish of S. Donato and then, a little before Rosa's birth, had moved to piazza delle Vigne. Thus Rosa was born in the parish of Our Lady delle Vigne

and was baptized in the parish of S. Donato.

§ 1029
Esteemed by all, even by opponents.

Ad 29, Proc. fol. 66: Although not seeking glory, she won the esteem of all, even of the opponents of her religious and political ideas. I must recall that in our family there was Federico Campanella, brother of our mother, who was a republican, an intimate follower of Giuseppe Mazzini.

He had also been a fellow student of Mgr. Salvatore Magnasco, afterward Archbishop of Genoa, with whom, with a certain frequency, as students, they went to visit Goffredo Mameli and his family, at Fontanegli, in Val Bisagno. My brother Federico too fought among the Garibaldians and Mazzinians, and was a Colonel of the General Staff of Giuseppe Garibaldi. For this reason my sister Rosa had to meet several times with personages of the party opposed to hers, who came to our house. She never yielded in matters of ideas, but by the sincerity of her faith, the delicacy of her manner and the goodness she showed in everything, she won from them too unlimited esteem. About the year 1868, for political reasons, there were imprisoned and taken to the prisons of Alessandria in the Bormida fortress my brother Federico, Stefano Canzio, Mosto, Pareto, Stallo.

§ 1030
Apostolate among political prisoners.

My sister, from Piacenza, hurried to Alessandria and, by her quality as mother of the nurses of St. Anne, was able to be the first to enter the prison and bring the due comforts to the political prisoners. This increased esteem for Rosa and won her the gratitude even of the advanced parties.

Ad 30: In her illness my sister showed a heroic strength of soul and unalterable serenity. She did not wish to be visited by Prof. Marchiafava, whom I had brought to her in the last days, and received him standing in her study. The last night I spent at her bed.

Ad 31: The corpse of my late sister remained well composed, presenting no particularity, except the swelling already brought on by the illness.

In the room where she had died, transformed into a modest funeral chamber, she was visited by many persons of every condition. At the funeral, held in the Church of the Sisters in Rome, via Merulana, a crowd of people came. So also the procession, in which I took part with my brother Federico, was made by very numerous people and by all the Institutes that she already had in Rome. She was buried provisionally in a niche of the Institute at Campo Verano, and afterward was transferred to the little Chapel built for the Institute in the same cemetery.

Ad 32: I add that she was transferred to the aforesaid Chapel because the aforementioned niche of the Institute was full of dampness; in the transfer the wooden coffin had to be broken up, the lead one remaining intact, because the wooden coffin was of too large a size and could not fit in the prepared niche. She was placed in the Chapel above the entrance door, facing the altar. From the wooden coffin two handles were removed, one of which the Sisters sent to me, and I still keep it.

§ 1032
Visits to the tomb.

Ad 34, Proc. fol. 69v.: I visited my sister's tomb repeatedly, both because I took care of the erection of the Institute's mortuary Chapel, and because, going to Rome, I almost never failed to visit my departed sister. I know that this tomb was and is still visited, besides by the Sisters, also by personages, both of the bourgeoisie and of the Genoese and Roman patriciate, also by those who did not have the same religious principles as the deceased, because she was widely known and esteemed by all who knew her.

Among those who are accustomed to visit my sister's tomb I recall the marchioness Carrega Emilia and the Princess Fitalia. I often found there Father Agostino Donadio, of the Minims of S. Francis of Paola.

§ 1033
Reputation for holiness.

Ad 35: Both during my sister's life and after her death she was surrounded with esteem and veneration among all. I cannot in particular testify to the esteem the Sisters had for her, because I had no special relations with them, except with Mother Carrega and with those forming part of the direction. On the other hand I heard very much talk with esteem from the laity, both from the people and from persons high in society, who often congratulated me on having such a sister, and I naturally was pleased at the esteem she enjoyed as a superior woman. I am not aware that anyone worked to create this esteem unduly for my sister; she, moreover, was most averse to seeking it. I recall in this connection that while her Sisters were working fruitfully in the care and education of abandoned girls in the Colony of Eritrea and in assisting the wounded, I observed to her that ample praises of the friars were made in the public papers and nothing was said of the sisters. She showed that she was pleased at that silence and that publicity would have displeased her. I also recall that once the publicist Odone, of ideas diametrically opposed to Rosa's, asked me whether I could procure him an interview with her, expressing however the fear of not being received because of the contrariety of his opinions. I put this wish to my sister, who showed herself ready to receive the journalist courteously on condition that no public praises be made of her.

Antequam prosequatur ad examen super Articulis, Judice ex officio, Proc. fol. 71, interrogat testem prout sequitur: Does the witness know, and how much does he know, about the dispute with the Priest Ricchini, custodian at S. Maria delle Grazie in Sampierdarena?

§ 1034
Conflict between the Servant of God and Fr. Ricchini.

Testis respondit: I know that the Priest Ricchini gave my sister a […] to shelter a certain number of girls; […]

sum I cannot determine precisely either the amount of the sum, I think thirty thousand lire, or the number of the girls, which I think was ten or twelve. Fr. Ricchini or his brother at first concerned themselves very directly with the house; which brought some inconvenience that my sister wished to remedy by removing outside interference from the house itself. Hence arose a conflict between my sister and the Priest Ricchini and still more with his brother. The dispute, as it seems to me, concerned the number of girls to be sheltered, which the Priest Ricchini perhaps claimed to be higher than the income from the donated sum. I recall that through, I believe, the brother of the said Priest insults against my sister were also written, which were afterward made to cease by my brother. I do not know how the dispute ended; I know that it was long and that my sister's side was upheld by our family Attorney Mr. Brignordello, a much esteemed person. Of the dispute no trace remained and the house of Sampierdarena always progressed, and now shelters about a hundred girls.

WITNESS III

§ 1042
The Servant of God was «a living rule».

Ad 19: The Venerated Foundress was Mother General of the Institute as long as she lived: she would have wished to lay down the office, but it was not permitted her; in my opinion she fulfilled this office with the utmost diligence, and one may say that she was so observant that one could call her «the living rule». At the beginning of the Institute she was a little easier in receiving the postulants who presented themselves, always however taking careful information and hearing the opinion of her assistants.

She visited frequently, especially at the beginning, the various houses of the Institute; she took care that religious discipline and observance of the Rule should flourish there, she insisted especially on meditation and wished that, before all, the local Superiors should give the example and then require that all the Sisters should make their meditation properly, because, she said, when meditation was well made the good course of the day was assured.

§ 1043
She governed prudently.

She was prudent and discreet in her government; she wanted the Superiors to be held by the Sisters in due honor, but she did not spare them the loving reproofs they had deserved, always however in such a way that their subordinates knew nothing of them.

For the various offices she tried to choose the most suitable and most worthy, without letting herself be guided by any particular affection.

§ 1044
Charity toward the Sisters.

Ad 20: The Servant of God took solicitous care that nothing should be lacking to the Sisters, and especially to the sickly and the ill, both in temporal and in spiritual things; as she had given the example, so she wanted the Superiors of the individual Houses to be for the Sisters, as she said, so many «Little Mothers», so that the religious, having left their mother and relatives, might find in the Superior a maternal affection and win her confidence and, receiving comfort in their sufferings, not feel the need to unburden themselves to others.

When the filial houses were in need, the Mother General always came to their aid; when instead they had a surplus, she advised paying it to the Generalate House, in order to be able to help the houses in want.

Likewise, if some wealthy Gentleman gave some sum that did not enter into the ordinary income of the Houses, she advised that it be given to the Generalate House for the aforesaid purposes.

She had similar care for the orphan and poor girls entrusted to the Institute and sent subsidies, as several times to me in the House of Cercola, so that for lack of means the Houses would not send away the girls sheltered.

§ 1049
Information on the austerity of the Servant of God,

Ad 1: Regarding the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno I know only the following, in relation to her great austerity of life. Being honorary physician to the Sisters of St. Anne of Genoa, and Mother General Rosa Gattorno being in Genoa in passing, I believe a year before her death, I was invited to visit her in the house of S. Silvestro; in the year of her death, a few months before her decease, I was called to Rome, I believe through the concern of the Sisters, to the convent in via Merulana, in consultation with the attending doctor.

Mother Rosa Gattorno was affected by nephritis, an illness which requires above all warmth and a rigorous diet. Instead I found the patient lying on a straw mattress and nourishing herself simply with soup in the strictest fast. Since the treatment, more than medicinal, had to be hygienic and dietetic, I prescribed her the use of wool and milk. But she refused both the one and the other, alleging that this was the way of life she had set herself and that she did not intend to modify it. On that occasion, precisely since it concerned nourishment, I took the liberty of pointing out to the Mother General that the Daughters of St. Anne, who are called to assist the sick during the night and especially during the long cold winter nights, cannot, because of the rigor of the […], comfort their stomach with anything, not even with […] of coffee; that this regime naturally turns out to be of grave harm […] to the health of the Sisters and that consequently it would have been good […] the rule somewhat. She answered me that this had been established and could not be modified.

I declare in an absolute way that I am not aware of […] that could refer to this cause.
