Let him also say whether the Servant of God experienced anxieties in this matter, which, from what causes; whether the Servant of God tried to free herself from these anxieties or from the institute to be founded, how, with which persons or whom, when, and let him report in everything the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

18. If the witness says, as the articles state, that the Servant of God undertook a journey to Rome to be exempted by the Supreme Pontiff, by his authority, from the institute to be founded, let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said how this came about, in what circumstances and with whom the journey to Rome was made, how long the Servant of God remained in Rome, how, with whom; what the same Servant of God did in Rome, whether she was received by the Supreme Pontiff, and how, what the Pontiff's own conduct toward her was and, conversely, what the Servant of God's conduct toward the Pontiff was. In narrating these things let the witness review the individual circumstances of things, places and persons, as well as the cause of his knowledge.

19. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said where finally the Servant of God founded the Institute. If he replies, as the articles state, that the Institute was founded at Piacenza, let him say whether the Servant of God did so of herself or at the request of someone or some persons, of whom or which, whether for this she sought the counsel of her Confessor and obtained the assent of the Ordinary of Piacenza.

Let him say whether the Servant of God suffered difficulties in founding the Institute, which, from whom, how the Servant of God extricated herself from these difficulties; by what means or by the work of which persons she made use to begin the work. In all this let him report all the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

20. Let the witness be asked whether he knows or heard it said on what day, month and year she actually founded the Institute she had proposed to found, with what title it was designated, whether this title was always the same or rather was changed to another, for what causes, how. Let him also say whether the Servant of God herself put on religious garb; if he replies that at the beginning of the foundation she put on religious garb after some interval of time, let him say for what causes she did so, when she finally laid aside secular dress.

Let him say whether the Servant of God chose the form of the garments she established for the religious sisters of her Institute.

In everything let him report the circumstances that seem opportune.

21. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said that the Servant of God provided, for the Institute founded by her, that particular Constitutions and Rules be drawn up, by whom or by which persons, how, when. If the witness replies, as the articles state, that the Servant of God herself finally undertook the burden of writing the Rules, let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether the Servant of God made use for this of the work or counsel of others; whether she experienced particular help from God; whether she sustained difficulties and from whom, which, how, for what causes; whether vows were prescribed in the same Rules and which, solemn or simple, temporary or perpetual. Let him also say whether she obtained approval for the Rules and from whom, whether from the Ordinary only or also from the Apostolic See; whether difficulties were raised by the Apostolic See; whether from it she obtained only the decree of praise or also approval, and in all this let him report the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

p. 672

22. Let the witness be asked whether he knows or heard it said who was the first governess of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. If the witness replies, as the articles state, that the Servant of God was the first governess of the same Institute, let him say how she undertook this office, whether spontaneously or compelled by obedience, by whom or by which persons, how long she held it; how she discharged the same office, whether she showed herself approachable; in admitting sisters or in receiving them, whether she sought and followed the votes of the other Sisters to whom this belongs.

Let him say whether she regularly visited the religious houses of her Institute and how, whether she watched assiduously that religious discipline be kept and flourish in them; whether she was always discreet and prudent; especially in assigning the various offices to the sisters, so that she always chose the more suitable and more worthy, without respect of persons. Let him say whether she took care that the necessities of life be supplied to the sisters subject to her, especially the sick and those suffering from poor health; whether, when these were in their last moments, she took care that at the opportune time the aids of the Church be administered to them.

In everything let him report the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

23. Let the witness be asked whether he knows or heard it said what the beginnings and growth of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne were, that is, whether in the beginnings the Servant of God suffered any troubles in spreading the Institute, which, from what causes, how, how long the troubles and contradictions lasted, whether afterward they came to an end and how. Let him say who were the fellow sisters whose work the Servant of God first used in the government and propagation of the Institute of the Sisters of St. Anne, in which places the Institute was spread in the lifetime of the Servant of God, what were the relations of the other religious houses with the generalate house, whether in what pertains to discipline or in administrative matters; whether the subject houses had to pay some sum, at fixed times, or in fact paid it to the generalate house; whether on this account the subject houses began to suffer some detriment; how in general the Servant of God behaved and watched over the administration of the goods of her Institute; whether she saw to it that necessities were not lacking not only to the Sisters but also to those who had been entrusted everywhere to the care of the Daughters of St. Anne, whether in spiritual goods or in temporal matters.

Let him report the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

24. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether an Apostolic Visitation ever took place in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; if affirmative, let him say for what reason, how long it lasted, what then was the Servant of God's conduct toward the Apostolic Visitor, whether she showed him due reverence and obedience and sincerely and candidly manifested everything that was to be manifested; what was the outcome of the Apostolic Visitation, what decrees were issued by the Visitor for the Institute; let him also say whether the Servant of God afterward strove that what had been prescribed by the Visitor be duly carried out,

25. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said what the Servant of God's conduct was, after the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, toward her children; whether she showed herself excessively solicitous for them, to the point of sometimes neglecting religious duties for them, or whether the same Servant of God's solicitude for her children turned out to the harm of the Institute

Let him state the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

26. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether the Servant of God, throughout the whole course of her life and in every state, kept the precepts of God and of the Church, as well as all that she was obliged to by reason of her state and according to circumstances; whether and how she fulfilled the vows and all the obligations to which she was bound by reason of the offices and institutions of which the preceding interrogatories treated. Specifically, let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether the Servant of God kept the rules of her Institute and took care that they be kept by others and how; whether she acted otherwise, in what, when, how often, in what circumstances, from what cause. In everything etc.

27. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said that the Servant of God shone with virtues, both theological, namely faith, hope, charity, and cardinal and those connected with them, namely prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, as well as humility, obedience, poverty and chastity.

Let him say whether she persevered in them until death. About each virtue in particular let him be asked, and of each let him narrate the individual acts, reporting all the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

28. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said that the Servant of God exercised the said virtues in the heroic degree, or not. If he affirms, let him say again whether she exercised all the virtues in the heroic degree, or only one or some, which. If the witness asserts either, let him be asked whether he knows what heroic virtue is and in what it consists and by what arguments he himself is moved to feel that all or some of the Servant of God's virtues were heroic, bringing the necessary and opportune arguments, circumstances and the cause of his knowledge. If, however, the witness does not know what heroic virtue is, let him be instructed by the Most Reverend Judges that heroic virtue is that which, either by the arduousness of the matter or by the manner, exceeds the common way of acting of pious men, and is recognized above all if in its exercise it is easy, if prompt, if cheerful.

29. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether the Servant of God in the exercise of the virtues exceeded the measure or not, whether she indulged in bodily affliction to excess or not, whether on that account she became less fit or unequal to fulfilling her duties or not. In everything etc.

30. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said that the Servant of God was ever enriched by God with supernatural gifts or charisms, namely of prophecy, reading of hearts, ecstasies, visions, apparitions and others of this kind.

And, should the witness affirm, let him also say which these were, when and with what she was endowed; whether she ever spoke, or not, of these gifts, and when; whether from necessity and which, or for the benefit of neighbors, and which, or by higher instinct and how, or rather from vainglory and for what reason, reporting in everything the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

31. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said that the Servant of God, while she lived, was enriched with the gift of miracles, or not. If the witness affirms, let him say which they were; and, if healings are in question, let him indicate the persons who by her work were restored to health, report the illnesses from which they recovered and the time those illnesses lasted, as well as the condition of the sick immediately before the healing. Finally, let him report all and each of the circumstances of the fact, place, time and persons, as well as the cause of his knowledge.

32. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether the Servant of God wrote anything, namely books, treatises, booklets, prayers, letters and other things of the kind. If he affirms, let him report, if possible, the names of those with whom such writings are kept and the places where they reside. Likewise let him say whether these writings contain anything contrary to sound doctrine and the commandments of God and the Church, or savoring of desire for vainglory, or anything else that in some way is contrary to heroic virtue, and what; reporting etc.

33. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said on what day, month, year and of what illness the Servant of God passed from this life. If the witness asserts it, let him say whether he knows or heard it said when the illness came on, how long and in what manner it lasted, whether the Servant of God herself predicted her own death, or not, when and how; whether the prediction was confirmed by the event or not; whether she suffered anything human or not and what; whether she prepared herself for death and how; whether, submissive to the divine will, she bore the pains of the illness patiently or not; whether in that time she said or did anything worthy of note and what; whether she uttered words of sorrow or indignation against anyone, against whom or which persons, when, how often, how; whether she asked for and received the Sacraments of the Church, which, when, how often, how; whether and what signs of a precious death she gave. In this regard etc.

34. Let him be asked in what condition the corpse of the Servant of God was; whether and where her funeral was celebrated, when, how; whether the people flocked or not to see the corpse and to the funeral. If the witness affirms it, let him also say where and when the concourse began, whether only common people flocked there or also men of more honorable condition; who and how many, for what cause; whether anything was done directly or indirectly to stir up the concourse and what, by whom or which persons, how, and let him report in everything the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

35. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said where, when, how the corpse of the Servant of God was buried; whether it remained there where first laid, or was transferred elsewhere and where, why, how, when, how often. Let him also be asked whether he knows or heard it said what is at present, and what was before, if a transfer occurred, the condition of the tomb which received the remains of the Servant of God; whether any inscription was placed or not and of what kind, where, when, to be reported as above etc.

36. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether in the very exposition of the corpse, or in the burial, or in the transfer, if one occurred, anything happened, or not, that bore the appearance of public and ecclesiastical cult, or of undue veneration, and what; whether anything of the kind exists or existed at the tomb of the Servant of God or elsewhere: where and what. If the witness denies it, let him produce arguments with which to support his denial. In everything, however, let him report the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

37. Let the witness be asked whether he ever went to visit the tomb of the Servant of God, why, how often, when; whether he knows or heard it said that others went or go there. If the witness affirms this, let him also say for what cause, and in what number they went or go there; whether this happens often or rarely, and when; whether these are only uneducated and common people, or also learned, serious and prudent men.

In this regard let the witness present the reason by which he affirms either, reporting also, if possible, the names at least of the principal ones. Likewise let him be asked when the concourse began, whether with the passing of time it was increased or rather diminished or interrupted; whether it ceased; why, how, when, for how long. Let him also say what its state is at present. Let him be asked, finally, whether he knows or heard it said whether there was or now is any effort to stir up the concourse itself

and what, reporting etc.

38. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said what opinion and reputation there was and is about the life, virtues, supernatural gifts and miracles of the Servant of God, whether while she lived or after her death. If the witness has said that a reputation for holiness flourished or flourishes concerning her, let him report the causes from which it arose. Let him also say whether it was increased or not, whether it was ever diminished, whether it ever ceased or not, when, how, why.

Let him also be asked where this reputation flourished and flourishes and among whom; that is, among serious, learned and religious men, or rather among the ignorant and common people. If he affirms the first, let him also review the names of the persons, if possible, unless he has already done so. Likewise let him be asked whether there was any effort or not, either to win such a reputation, or to conceal something that could diminish or wholly remove such an opinion; what, by the work of whom or which persons. Let him say, finally, what the witness himself thinks of this reputation, and let him report in everything the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge.

39. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether anything was ever said, done or written, or not, against the Servant of God's virtues and reputation for holiness, whether while she lived or after her death. Let him say, namely, whether there was or is anyone who doubted or doubts the holiness of her life, or who had or has an opinion altogether contrary. If the witness hints that there existed or exist someone or some who dissented from the opinion on her holiness, let him say: who they were or are, let him report their names and surnames, and the place where they live, if they are alive. Let him likewise declare why these deny the Servant of God's virtues and judged or still judge the said reputation false, or doubtful, or suspect, or undeserved.

It will moreover be for the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Judge Ordinary or the Most Reverend Judges Delegate to subject these adversaries to examination ex officio, whether few or many, if they have not been brought forward by the Postulator, administering to them the oath to tell the truth and to keep secrecy, by which they at the same time declare that they come to the examination neither from hatred, nor from enmity, nor for any private cause, but solely in obedience to the truth. This they will do, like the other witnesses, according to the VI interrogatory and also afterward, if need be. Furthermore, let them inquire diligently from them what they thought against the reputation for holiness and virtues of the Servant of God. If, however, the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Judge Ordinary or the Most Reverend Judges Delegate find that these contrary witnesses have died, or for another most grave cause cannot be present, let them order the Postulator to produce an authentic document either of their death or of the impossibility of undergoing examination, to be inserted in the process.

40. Let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether after the death of the Servant of God any grace or miracle was wrought by almighty God, in regard to her or by her intercession.

That the witness may explain the matter fully, let him be instructed that a grace is a work of nature augmented by God; a miracle, however, is a work to be attributed to divine power alone, such as preservation from an evil which by the laws of nature would certainly have befallen, or healing from some illness so grave that it can be removed only by God's help, at least as to the manner. These things having been explained, let the witness report the fact or facts which in the case he judges graces or miracles, reviewing the circumstances and the cause of knowledge etc.

41. If the witness has reported one or more healings as miracles obtained through the intercession of the Servant of God, let him be asked: whether he knows or heard it said whether any extrajudicial attestation or attestations were made, or not, on this matter. If the witness affirms, let him say by whom or which persons, when, in what manner. Let him report where it or they are, with whom or which persons. If he says he has some attestation, whether autograph or a copy, let him exhibit it in the acts. If, however, the attestation or attestations are asserted by the Postulator of the Cause, let the Most Reverend Judges require them; if they are in the hands of others, let them subject these to examination, as far as possible.

42. If the witness says that through the intercession of the Servant of God there occurred the healing or healings reported in the Articles, or others which are held to be miracles, let him report all the circumstances of each, narrating the name, surname, native land, age, condition and state of the healed person, as well as the place and time at which the healing itself occurred.

Therefore, about each healing let the witness be asked whether he knows or heard it said what the constitution and habit of body of the sick person was; what illnesses or illness; when and how they began and lasted, what their symptoms, what changes, what course; whether and which physicians or surgeons attended the sick person, or not, when, for how long; whether and what their diagnosis and prognosis was, that is, what judgment they made of the illnesses themselves and of their outcome; whether drugs or remedies were applied or not, which and when; whether and what these achieved, when, how; and let him report the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge, as above.

43. If, however, a woman is in question, let him also be asked whether he knows or heard it said whether she was subject to convulsions and hysterical passion, or not, when, for how long, how; whether the menstrual purgations proceeded regularly in her or not, and in what manner, if by age she were subject to them; especially, however, how these behaved in the days close to the healing and afterward, reporting etc.

44. Furthermore, let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said in what state the sick person was a little before the healing; whether there occurred a good crisis or not, when and what; whether the healing in question happened gradually or in an instant and how; whether a relapse followed afterward or not, when and what; whether a metastasis occurred or not, that is, a conversion of the former illness into another, which, when, how; whether the healing itself was perfect or not and why; and let him report etc.

45. Let him be asked whether and by what arguments the invocation of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno is established; whether and why the healing itself is to be attributed to her intercession alone and not to another, whether Saint, or Blessed, or Servant of God, reporting as above etc.

46. Lastly, let him be asked whether he knows or heard it said what the opinion of such a healing was and is, especially among physicians and surgeons; what the parents of the healed person, or others who attended him, thought of it; what the witness himself thinks in this matter, and let him report the individual circumstances and the cause of his knowledge, as above.

If the witness has mentioned anyone or some, especially among the physicians and surgeons, who were in doubt about the alleged prodigious healing, or attributed it to nature or art, let the Most Reverend Judges Delegate inquire of these contrary men and subject them to examination, for the same reason set out above in interrogatory 39. If, however, the healed person is still alive, and the gravity of the fact seems to deserve altogether careful investigation, it will be for the Most Reverend Judges to subject him or her to the examination of two of the more renowned physicians or surgeons, upright and religious, who have not testified in this process, so that it may be evident how he or she is at present, and whether they were perfectly healed of the illness or illnesses from which they came out free by miracle.

In this regard these experts shall first take an oath, before the same Most Reverend Judges, to fulfill faithfully the office entrusted to them.

Then, as they judge best, let them inspect the healed person diligently, jointly if possible, and they shall question him or her opportunely. Afterward, however, let them set forth before the same Judges, orally and singly, whatever they have found, after having again taken the oath to tell the truth and keep secrecy about what they are to report. Their answers let the Notary record in the acts, as was said above about the other witnesses.

47. Finally, let any witness be asked whether he knows anything beyond what he has so far said, either because it afterward came to mind after the answers were given, or because he was not specifically asked about it. This, however, concerns not only the virtues and deeds of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, but also her alleged supernatural gifts, miracles and reputation for holiness.

Let him likewise be asked whether there is anything in his testimony that he thinks should be amended. If the witness assents, let him report the omissions and plainly amend whatever he thinks should be corrected or amended, explaining the circumstances and the cause of his knowledge, as has been continually noted.

For the rest, let the religious conscience, care and knowledge of the Most Reverend Judges Delegate supply, who, together with the undersigned, are to have joint power to add other questions as the case may be, if they judge it better in the Lord

Rome, 5 April 1913

Fr. IOANNES LUCCHETTI

BRIEF BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES ON THE PROMINENT PERSONS

MOST OFTEN ENCOUNTERED IN THE «SUMMARIUM»

ALIMONDA Gaetano, cardinal. Born at Genoa on 23 October 1818 and died there on 31 May 1891. He was ordained priest in 1843; in 1864 he showed himself one of the greatest orators of his time. He was consecrated bishop of Albenga in 1877 and in 1879 was created cardinal; from 1883 until death he was archbishop of Turin. In 1880 he had been named Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne and always showed the Servant of God great esteem, as appears from the correspondence preserved in the Historical Archive of the Institute.

BARBIELLINI AMIDEI Gaspare, son-in-law of the Servant of God. Born in Rome, son of Count Cesare, on 6 July 1851 and died on 26 September 1931. In 1876 he married Carlotta Custo, daughter of the Servant of God. Entrusted with various affairs of the Institute, he showed himself greedy for money and was an occasion for the Servant of God to exercise heroically the virtue of fortitude.

BERARDI Giuseppe, cardinal. Born at Ceccano (Frosinone) on 28 September 1810; died in Rome on 6 September 1878. Having become a celebrated lawyer, he entered the magistracy and, after the premature death of his wife and daughter, in 1844 put on the ecclesiastical habit. In 1851 he was named secretary of the Congregation for Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs and consultor of various congregations; in 1859 he became pro-secretary of state; in 1862 he was consecrated bishop and in 1868 was created cardinal; he was a personal friend of St. John Bosco. From 1875 until death he was Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne and nourished for the Servant of God particular benevolence and esteem.

BERNARDINO of Portogruaro (Giuseppe Dal Vago), Servant of God. Born on 15 January 1822 at Portogruaro; died at Quaracchi on 7 May 1895. In 1839 he entered the novitiate of the Reformed Franciscans and was ordained priest in 1844. In 1862 he was elected procurator general of the Reformed and in 1869 Pius IX named him general of the whole Franciscan Order. He founded the St. Bonaventure institute at Quaracchi and the international college of St. Anthony in Rome. He succeeded in giving new impetus to the Order, disturbed by the suppressions, and to its missions; he personally visited the Minorite provinces. In 1889 he left the generalate and was consecrated bishop of Sardica. For some years he was spiritual director of the Servant of God.

CAMPANELLA Federico, maternal uncle of the Servant of God. Born at Genoa on 10 July 1804; died at Florence on 9 December 1884. During his studies he made friends with Giuseppe Mazzini and the Ruffini brothers and, after taking a degree in law, directed the Genoese section of Young Italy. In 1833 the police discovered the revolutionary plots and he was forced to flee into exile; a faithful collaborator of Mazzini, he had however some disagreements with him. He returned to Italy in 1844 and took part in the insurrections of Milan and Genoa of 1848-49: condemned to death in absentia, he fled to Rome and took part in the defense of the city. In 1862 he was elected deputy. In 1868 he received the office of grand master of the Grand Orient of Palermo; three years later he was elected honorary grand master. He always frequented with assiduity and affection the family of his sister Maria Adelaide, married to Francesco Gattorno, and had considerable influence on his nephews, above all on Federico, who followed in his footsteps.

CELESIA Michelangelo, cardinal. Born at Palermo on 13 January 1814; died there on 15 April 1904. A Benedictine, he was for eight years Abbot general of the Cassinese Congregation; in 1860 he was named bishop of Patti and in 1871 was transferred to the Archbishopric of Palermo; in 1884 he was created cardinal. In 1880 he welcomed the Daughters of St. Anne into the city and diocese of Palermo and from then on came to know the Servant of God and to hold her in esteem.

CHARVAZ Andrea, bishop. Born on 25 December 1793 at Hautecourt, died at Mont-Saint-Michel near Moûtiers on 18 October 1870. Charles Albert wanted him as tutor of his sons Vittorio Emanuele and Ferdinando. In 1834 he was elected bishop of Pinerolo; he was a member of the king's privy council and then of the new council of state; in protest against the laws on the press he left the episcopal see and took refuge in Rome; in 1853 he was made bishop of Genoa. In the new diocese he took care of the formation of the clergy, favored all works of charity, protected the religious congregations. He had the greatest esteem for the Servant of God and encouraged her to carry out the new foundation and, to this end, directed her to Pius IX, from whom he obtained her an audience.

COGROSSI Luigi, priest. Born at Castelleone (Cremona) on 25 April 1806; died in Rome on 19 February 1885. Ordained priest at Piacenza in 1831, he returned to his native town. Around 1860 a reputation as a healer had grown up around him, which provoked appeals to the bishop; advised to leave the diocese, he began to travel through Italy. In 1864 he met the Servant of God at Genoa, who began to confess to him, struck by the reputation for holiness that surrounded him; he helped and counseled her in the beginnings of the foundation of the Institute. In 1867 the Servant of God had to reconsider her opinion of him and thought it right, for herself and for the Institute, to remove him decisively. After this event Cogrossi settled in Rome and was canon of the Church of S. Maria Regina Coeli in Monte Santo. CUSMANO Giacomo, blessed. Born at Palermo on 15 March 1834 and died there on 14 March 1888. Formerly a physician, he became a priest in 1860. He founded the association of the «Morsel of the Poor»; around 1880 he turned to the Servant of God to have sisters for his work: the negotiation did not conclude favorably, so he himself founded a new congregation: the Servants of the Poor, and seven years later the Missionary Servants of the Poor. In 1880 he gave hospitality to the first community of the Daughters of St. Anne in Palermo, led by the Servant of God Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi.

DI FRANCIA Annibale, venerable. Born at Messina on 5 July 1851, died there on 1 June 1927. Of noble family and fervent intellect, having become a priest in 1878, he at once devoted himself to works of charity and founded the Antonian orphanages for boys and girls; for the latter he would have wanted the Daughters of St. Anne and asked them of the Servant of God, but the negotiation had no favorable outcome, so he founded the Rogationist sisters and associated them with the Rogationist priests founded by himself.

DUSMET Giuseppe Benedetto, venerable. Born at Palermo on 15 August 1818, died at Catania on 4 April 1894. Educated by the Benedictine monks, he professed their rule. Ordained priest in 1842, he was named archbishop of Catania in 1867 and in 1888 was created cardinal. He had occasion to know the Servant of God, who had opened communities in the diocese of Catania, and admired her humility (cf. Summ., p. 272).

FRANCESCO MARIA of Camporosso, saint. Born at Camporosso (Imperia) on 27 December 1804, died at Genoa on 17 September 1866. He entered the Capuchin Order as a lay brother and lived in the convent of the Conception in Genoa. He sanctified himself in toil and penance, in silence and humility; he carried out a vast charitable work in the harbor district and was commonly called the Holy Father. The Servant of God turned to him for counsel when she was thinking of the foundation of the Institute and received from him encouragement together with the prophecy of grave sufferings which she would have to

face.

FRASSINETTI Giuseppe, Servant of God. Born at Genoa on 15 December 1804 and died there on 2 January 1868; he is the brother of St. Paola. Ordained priest in 1827, he exercised his ministry first at Quarto al Mare, then in Genoa, where he was prior of S. Sabina. Tireless in pastoral activity, he supported and founded very many associations; he zealously promoted frequent communion. He ordered the rules of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate of Mornese and founded a group of this association in Genoa, of which the Servant of God also was a member, and whom in 1863 or 64 he insistently asked to become its president; on this occasion he also asked her to obtain from the archbishop approval of the rule which he had transformed into the «Rule of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, the new Ursulines». The Servant of God, by order of Mgr. Charvaz, corrected the rule, which was thus approved. To pastoral activity Frassinetti added that of writer on pastoral asceticism and moral theologian.

GATTORNO Federico, brother of the Servant of God. Born at Genoa on 13 January 1836, died in Rome on 17 June 1913. Patriot and conspirator, enrolled in freemasonry, he took part in the movement of Genoa of 1849; traveling in the East because of his trade, he never ceased to make proselytes for the Italian cause. In 1859, being on the Black Sea, the news reached him of Garibaldi's landing in Sicily: he at once armed a ship at his own expense and went to join the expedition with 150 young men whom he had gathered. Afterward he was always at Garibaldi's side: in 1862 at Aspromonte, in 1866 in the Trentino, in 1870 in France where he was promoted colonel; in 1896 he fought in Greece. In 1900 he was elected republican deputy for Rimini and remained in the chamber until death. He was always bound by most lively affection to the Servant of God, whom he generously helped in many affairs of the Institute.

GIANNOTTI Donato, Servant of God. Born at Casapulla (Caserta) on 18 June 1828, died at Santa Maria Capua Vetere (Caserta) on 26 February 1914. Ordained priest, he exercised fruitfully the ministry of preaching and spiritual direction. Under the guidance of the venerable Fr. Ludovico of Casoria he founded at Santa Maria Capua Vetere a boys' orphanage directed by the Gray Friars of Charity, of whom he became an auxiliary tertiary. He founded the women's congregation of the Handmaids of Mary. From about 1881 he was in relation with the Servant of God and a reciprocal esteem and veneration bound them.

GRANITO PIGNATELLI DI BELMONTE Gennaro, cardinal. Born at Naples on 10 April 1851, died in Rome on 16 February 1948. Ordained priest in 1879, he carried out an effective apostolate in the diocese; in 1893 he was called as minutante to the Congregation for Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs; he fulfilled various diplomatic assignments and in 1899 was consecrated bishop and sent as apostolic nuncio to Brussels. In 1904 he was transferred to the nunciature of Vienna and in 1911 was created cardinal. While not yet a priest he had known the Servant of God, for whom he had great esteem and veneration. After ordination he became her counselor both for the affairs of the Institute and for matters concerning her spirit. Under the guidance of the Servant of God he had tried to begin a congregation of priests called «Sons of St. Anne», but met the opposition of his own archbishop.

LUDOVICO of Casoria, venerable. Born at Casoria (Naples) on 11 March 1814, died at Naples on 30 March 1885. In 1859 he founded the congregation of the Friars of Charity called Gray Friars, to which he added the Gray Sisters of Elizabeth. He created numerous works for orphans, the elderly, the blind and deaf-mutes. He knew and met the Servant of God several times when she opened communities in the city and province of Naples.

RAMPOLLA DEL TINDARO Mariano, cardinal. Born on 17 August 1843 at Polizzi, died on 16 December 1913 in Rome. Priest in 1866, bishop and apostolic nuncio in Madrid in 1882; in 1887 he was created cardinal and named secretary of state. In 1899, on the occasion of the episcopal ordination of Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, he met the Servant of God and agreed to be protector of the Institute, encouraging and supporting the Servant of God in the last months of her life.

RANZA Antonio, bishop. Born at Piacenza on 15 January 1801, died at Piacenza on 20 November 1875. He completed his studies at the Alberoni College; he was professor of philosophy and theology at the episcopal seminary, librarian of the civic library, canon of the cathedral. A representative of the intransigent clergy and most faithful to the temporal power of the popes, he was named bishop of Piacenza in 1849. He received two convictions from the civil tribunal, but recent studies have scaled down the accusations of lack of patriotism. In 1866 he welcomed into the diocese the Servant of God who was beginning the foundation at Piacenza; though keeping at first a prudent attitude, he encouraged and supported her in the many difficulties of the first years of the Institute's life and praised her several times in his correspondence with the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars.

SANFELICE Guglielmo, cardinal. Born at Aversa on 18 April 1834, died at Naples on 3 January 1897. He studied at the abbey of Cava dei Tirreni where he became a monk and priest. In 1878 he succeeded Card. Sisto Riario Sforza as archbishop of Naples and in 1884 was created cardinal. He distinguished himself by his pastoral gifts and by great charity on the occasion of natural calamities. He knew and esteemed the Servant of God who had opened several communities in the Neapolitan diocese.

SCALABRINI Giovanni Battista, venerable. Born at Fino Mornasco (Como) on 8 July 1839, died at Piacenza on 1 June 1905. Ordained priest in 1863, he was rector of the seminary from 1867 to 1870. Preconized bishop of Piacenza in 1875, in thirty years of episcopate he showed tireless zeal, distinguishing himself particularly by diocesan synods, Eucharistic worship, the spread of catechetical teaching and care of Italian emigrants. He founded the Missionaries of St. Charles, men and women. From the time he took possession of the diocese he held great esteem for the Servant of God; in 1891 he wanted the Daughters of St. Anne beside his missionaries in New York; at the beginning of the foundation of the women Missionaries he had recourse several times to the Servant of God so that one of her sisters might direct the nascent community.

SERAFINI Domenico, cardinal. Born in Rome on 3 August 1852, died there on 3 March 1918. At 19 he entered the monastery of S. Scholastica at Subiaco and in 1877 was ordained priest. He had important assignments in the Order and in 1896 was elected abbot general. In 1900 he became bishop of Spoleto; in 1912 he was named assessor of the Congregation of the Holy Office and in 1914 created cardinal; from that year he was first pro-prefect and then prefect of the Congregation of Propaganda Fide. From 1898 to 1903 he was apostolic visitor of the Daughters of St. Anne, hence he knew the Servant of God; in the concluding report presented to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars he attests the rectitude of the Servant of God.

TESTA Angelo, priest. Born at Castelnuovo Fogliani (Piacenza) on 16 May 1788, died at Piacenza on 29 November 1873. A pupil of the episcopal seminary and the Alberoni College, he took degrees at Parma in theology and law. He was a teacher in the seminary and canon and then provost of the cathedral. His profound culture, his experience in governing the Cathedral Chapter and his Thomist orientation led the new bishop Ranza to appoint him his vicar. Canon Testa welcomed with favor the Servant of God's foundation in the city of Piacenza and was generous to her in support and encouragement.

TORNATORE Giovanni Battista, co-founder of the Daughters of St. Anne. Born at Dolceacqua (Imperia) on 11 April 1820, died at Piacenza on 31 January 1895. Having entered the Congregation of the Mission in Rome, he was ordained priest in 1844. While still a student he formed a friendship with the venerable Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi OM, of whom he was afterward also confessor. From 1852 to 1876 he was professor at the Alberoni College of Piacenza. After leaving public teaching he published some works of theology. When the Servant of God went to Piacenza to begin the foundation of the Institute, Tornatore began to collaborate with her and influenced decisively the name and spirit of the Institute, whose Rules he wrote. He was always recognized as superior of the Institute in temporalibus. In 1888 he was removed because the presence of two authorities threatened to create division in the Institute, but Tornatore continued to benefit the Daughters of St. Anne until death. The special Chapter of 1969-1971 recognized him as co-founder. VANNICELLI CASONI Luigi, cardinal. Born at Amelia on 16 April 1801, died in Rome on 21 April 1877. Vatican canon in 1829, in 1835 he became vice-commissioner of the four Legations with residence in Bologna and in 1838 vice-chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, governor of Rome, president of the Tribunal of the government. In 1842 he was created cardinal and Legate in Bologna; in 1850 the Pontiff elected him archbishop of Ferrara; in 1870 he was named pro-datary while continuing to govern the diocese of Ferrara. He carried out, both in Bologna and in Ferrara, intense pastoral and charitable activity. He was the first Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne and was of great help to the Servant of God.
